A test asserting the function raises or refuses such input would catch this behavior if it were wrong; absent that, the omission of path confinement can ship silently.

findings.title: Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report before serialising it. Both the import and the loop were deleted, so `Report.get(rid)` results are now returned for any `rid` the caller supplies, with no comparison of `report.tenant_id` against `user.tenant_id`. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and read another tenant's data. The retrieved docstring for `require_owner` states explicitly that every cross-tenant object read must go through it, so this endpoint no longer meets the documented contract.

Note also that `user = current_user(request)` on line 5 is now dead — its result is unused — which is the tell that the authorization step is simply gone rather than relocated.

If the motivation was performance, keep the control and fix the cost instead: fetch the reports with a tenant-scoped query (e.g. `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the filter happens in one round trip, and treat any requested id not returned as forbidden/not-found rather than silently omitted.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: Removed authz check has no test guarding against regression
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner() call from bulk_export, eliminating the tenant-ownership check on each report before export. No test file is part of this PR, so there is nothing that would fail if a user requests report_ids belonging to another tenant. Given require_owner exists specifically to prevent cross-tenant access (per api/auth.py docstring), this behavior change should be covered by a test that asserts Forbidden is raised (or reports are excluded) when report_ids includes objects from a different tenant.

findings.title: Public bulk_export lacks authorization contract documentation
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function is a public API endpoint that now accepts `report_ids` from any caller without documenting who is permitted to access each report. After the removal of `require_owner`, it is unclear whether callers can export reports they do not own. A competent caller reviewing the signature alone cannot determine the authorization boundary. Either restore the check and document the rejection case, or add a docstring explicitly stating that the function exports any reports by ID regardless of ownership (if that is intentional).

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` composes its query with an f-string, splicing `term` and `status` straight into the statement inside single quotes, then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params`. Any caller value containing a quote breaks out of the literal: e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%' UNION SELECT ... --"` lets the caller choose the projected columns or append further statements depending on the driver's multi-statement handling.

The fix matches the function directly above it on line 5 and the contract documented in `billing/db.py` ("`params` must carry every caller value"):

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = ("SELECT * FROM customers "
           "WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s")
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter value*, not in the SQL text, so the `LIKE` pattern stays parameterised.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute(sql, params=None)` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that (`%s` placeholder plus a tuple). `search_customers` instead embeds `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params at all.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is wrong for benign inputs:

- Any value containing an apostrophe (e.g. `term="O'Brien"`, a very ordinary customer name) closes the quote early and the statement fails to parse \u2014 a runtime error, not a filtered result.
- `%` and `_` in `term` are LIKE metacharacters and are not escaped, so `term="50%"` silently matches far more rows than intended.

Rewrite to match line 5's pattern and let the driver bind the values, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If leading/trailing wildcards should not be user-controllable, escape `%`/`_` in `term` before wrapping it.

findings.title: No test exists for search_customers, masking SQL injection defect
findings.body: search_customers builds a query via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into SQL text, unlike get_customer which parameterises correctly. There is no test in this diff exercising search_customers, so nothing would fail or flag that user input is concatenated unsafely into SQL. A test asserting that execute() is called with a parameterised query (and untouched literal SQL string) would have caught this regression at review time.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no parsing, scheme restriction, or host allowlist. The function immediately above it in the same file (lines 8-10) demonstrates the control that is expected here: it resolves the host and raises `ValueError("destination not allowed")` unless the host is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. The new entry point bypasses that control entirely.

Sink: `requests.get(url, timeout=5)` on line 14. Entry point: the `url` parameter, which per the PR description is the customer-registered webhook target — i.e. attacker-controlled. Consequences of an unauthenticated or low-privilege caller controlling this value:

- Internal network and cloud metadata reachability (`http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:<port>/...`), with the HTTP status code returned to the caller acting as an oracle for port/endpoint existence.
- Non-HTTP schemes: `requests` with the default adapters will also handle `file://` if a file adapter is mounted, and scheme confusion is avoidable cheaply — reject anything that is not `http`/`https` explicitly.

Fix: route this through the same validation used by the send path — parse the URL, require `http`/`https`, resolve the host and enforce `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (and reject private/link-local address literals), and pass `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted host cannot 302 the request onto an internal target.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced above
findings.body: The delivery function immediately above rejects any URL whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before calling `requests.post`. `verify_endpoint` performs the same kind of server-side fetch on a caller-supplied URL with no host or scheme check at all, so the invariant the module establishes on line 8-9 no longer holds for every outbound request in this file. Extract the host check into a helper and call it from both functions (and pass `allow_redirects=False`, since a 302 from an allowed host would otherwise re-introduce the same gap in the post path's model).

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test and lacks the allowlist check used elsewhere
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a server-side GET to a caller-supplied URL without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check applied a few lines above for the POST path. There is no test in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so a regression (e.g. someone assuming it already validates the host, or a future refactor that breaks the intended behavior) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation of contract
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` accepts a URL parameter and performs a network request, but has no docstring explaining what it does, what the URL should be, or what the caller should expect from the return value. A competent caller might assume it returns a boolean (True/False for valid/invalid) rather than an HTTP status code, or might not know if it validates the URL against any allowlist before fetching it (unlike the existing `send_webhook` function on line 10). Add a docstring clarifying the function's purpose, parameter constraints, and return type.

findings.title: Public access block fully disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. These four settings are the guardrail that prevents any ACL or bucket policy — added later, by any principal with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutBucketAcl`, or by a copy-paste of the `assets` policy — from making objects world-readable. With them off, a single subsequent ACL or policy change silently exposes customer invoices to anonymous readers, and `ignore_public_acls = false` means object-level ACLs set by uploaders are honoured too.

This block appears to have been copied from the `assets` resource above, where public access is intentional. For `invoices`, either delete the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource entirely (the account-level block then applies) or, preferably, declare it explicitly with all four values set to `true`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ invoices bucket disables all S3 public access protections

findings.title: Signature compared with == instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a copy of `verify_stripe` except that the final comparison uses `==`. `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the time taken to reject a candidate signature leaks how many leading hex characters were correct. An attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries can recover the expected digest byte-by-byte and then forge arbitrary payloads for this provider. Replace line 12 with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the pattern already established on line 7.

Secondary consequence of the same line: the two functions now also behave differently on malformed input. `hmac.compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None` or a non-ASCII `str`, whereas `expected == header` quietly returns `False`. Whichever behaviour callers rely on, it should be the same for both providers; switching to `compare_digest` makes them consistent.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test exists to catch verify_acmepay's unsafe comparison
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new, security-sensitive code (webhook signature verification) but has no accompanying test in this diff. Without a test asserting behavior on valid/invalid signatures, a regression like the use of == instead of hmac.compare_digest (as seen here) would ship silently. Since verify_stripe presumably has some test coverage given it's the established pattern, the new function should have equivalent coverage.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body and logged the detail server-side. It now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response body. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an exception (malformed input, oversized payload, bad content type, a DB timeout) receives file system paths, module and function names, library versions implied by frame paths, and frequently fragments of the offending data — SQL text from a DBAPI error, connection strings from a driver error, or key material embedded in a message from a crypto library. That is direct reconnaissance value for an attacker mapping the service, and in some cases an outright secret disclosure.

Keep the detail where it already goes: `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already captures the full traceback server-side. Restore the opaque client body, and if debugging correlation is the goal, generate a request/error ID, log it alongside the exception, and return only that ID to the caller. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that defaults to off rather than making it the unconditional behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and yields "NoneType: None" outside a handler

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape changed: fixed message replaced by variable text plus new key

findings.title: Public error handler lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler that now returns exception details and tracebacks to clients. Without a docstring explaining what this function does, what it accepts, and what it returns, callers cannot understand the contract. The fact that it now exposes internal exception text and full tracebacks to clients is a significant behavior change that should be explicitly documented so callers understand they are receiving sensitive internals.

findings.title: No test guards response contents of handle()
findings.body: The handle() function's return value changed from a generic error message to one containing the raw exception string and full traceback. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this response body changed again (e.g., reverted, or expanded further) or if it started leaking more/less information. A test asserting on the exact structure of the returned tuple/dict (e.g., that it does NOT contain 'traceback' or arbitrary exception internals) would catch regressions here.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is fast and hardware-accelerated, so an attacker holding the hash table can brute-force or rainbow-table these values essentially for free, and identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts. The module already has the right primitive one function above it: reuse `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` (or delegate to `hash_password`) for anything that ends up in the password column, and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. If this value is actually meant to be a short-lived reset *token* rather than a stored password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and hash it with SHA-256, and rename the function so it cannot be mistaken for password storage.

The caller is not in this diff, so I cannot confirm where the digest is persisted or compared \u2014 but the name and the `raw` password argument make password storage the plain reading.

findings.title: Public password function contract unclear: MD5 weakness undocumented
findings.body: `hash_reset_password` is a public function that hashes passwords using MD5, a cryptographically weak algorithm unsuitable for password storage. The function name and signature do not communicate this critical security distinction from the correct `hash_password` function above it, which uses bcrypt. A caller could easily confuse these two functions or assume the function provides password-grade security. At minimum, the function needs a docstring explicitly stating that it uses MD5 and should not be used for storing passwords, or the implementation should be corrected to use a proper password hashing algorithm.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with existing bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-character MD5 hex digest with no salt and no algorithm prefix. If both values are written to the same stored-credential field, the existing verification path will either raise or silently fail for every account that went through the reset flow, and there is no marker in the stored value that lets a caller tell the two encodings apart. Reset passwords should go through `hash_password` (or the stored value must carry an explicit scheme tag that the verifier dispatches on).

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new function introduced in this diff with no accompanying test. Nothing would fail if its implementation were changed to something incorrect, insecure, or simply broken (e.g. returning a constant, throwing on certain inputs, or being swapped for a different hash algorithm). Since this touches the password reset path, add at least a basic test asserting the function returns a deterministic hash of the input.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the repository's default (typically write) permissions, and it is triggered by pull requests from forks with no approval gate. Lines 11-12 then deliberately check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` *from that checkout*, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on lines 14-15.

Entry point: any unauthenticated GitHub user opens a PR from a fork containing a modified `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, plus package manifests / lifecycle scripts it may invoke). Sink: the `run` step, executing as a privileged job. The attacker gets `NPM_TOKEN` (publish rights on the npm package) and the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and can push commits, alter releases, or poison caches.

Remedies, in order of preference:
- Revert to `pull_request`. If the size check only reads the diff, it does not need base-repo secrets at all. Only the NPM_TOKEN requirement suggests otherwise — if the script needs a registry token merely to install dependencies, use a read-only token and keep the untrusted trigger.
- If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required, do **not** check out the head SHA and do not execute anything from it. Split into two workflows: an untrusted `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and holds the secrets.
- At minimum, add an explicit `permissions:` block scoped to the least privilege needed, and gate the job behind an environment requiring reviewer approval for first-time/outside contributors.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Measurement now runs on head commit, not the merge result
findings.body: With the previous `pull_request` trigger, `actions/checkout` defaults to the PR *merge* commit (`refs/pull/N/merge`), so the size measurement reflected what the repository would look like after merging. Pinning `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha` measures the fork's head commit in isolation, which diverges from the merge result whenever the base branch has moved. Size numbers reported on the PR (and any threshold gating built on them) will silently be computed against a stale base. If the intent is to keep measuring the merged state, check out the base and merge, or keep the merge-ref behaviour.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs the base branch's workflow file
findings.body: `pull_request_target` always evaluates the workflow definition from the base branch, not from the PR head. This change therefore will not take effect for the PR that introduces it, and future edits to `.github/workflows/size.yml` will not be exercised by CI before merge. Also note the check name/context reported to branch protection comes from a different event now; if `size` is a required status check, confirm the required-context configuration still matches after the trigger change.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values; hashable-but-unserialisable now raises
findings.body:
The previous key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which accepted any context whose values were hashable and comparable. The new key runs `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which accepts only JSON-serialisable values. Template contexts very commonly carry `datetime`, `Decimal`, sets, or domain objects with a `__str__` \u2014 all hashable, none JSON-serialisable \u2014 and every such call now raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from inside `cached_render`, converting a working render into a hard failure.

Two secondary edge cases from the same line: `sort_keys=True` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'` for a context with mixed-type keys, and int key `1` vs string key `"1"` both serialise to `"1"`, silently colliding into one cache entry.

If the digest form is wanted, pass `default=repr` (or a `cls=` encoder) to `json.dumps` so unserialisable values degrade to a stable string instead of raising, and confirm no caller passes non-string context keys.

findings.title: No test that different template_source values produce different cache entries
findings.body: The new key derivation hashes `[template_source, context]` together. All new tests vary only `context` while holding `template_source` constant (`"{{ a }}"`). There is no test asserting that two calls with the same context but different `template_source` are treated as distinct cache entries — a regression that swapped the digest to hash only `context` (or mishandled the list ordering) would still pass every test in this file.

findings.title: Switch to json.dumps changes serializability requirements for context, untested
findings.body: The old implementation keyed on `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which only required context values to be sortable/hashable. The new implementation requires the entire context to be JSON-serializable via `json.dumps`. Any caller previously passing non-JSON-serializable but hashable/orderable values (e.g. tuples, custom objects with __lt__) would now raise TypeError instead of caching successfully. No test exercises this behavior change or documents the new constraint.

findings.title: directory is no longer shell-split or glob-expanded
findings.body: Under the old `shell=True` form, `directory` was handed to `/bin/sh`, so any caller passing a glob (`/srv/data/*`), multiple paths (`/srv/a /srv/b`), or a `~` prefix had those expanded/split by the shell before `tar` saw them. In the list form `directory` is exactly one argv element, so `tar` receives the literal string and will fail with "Cannot stat: No such file or directory" (then `check=True` raises `CalledProcessError`). If any existing caller relies on that expansion this is a silent runtime break, not a rejected input. Please confirm every call site passes a single literal path, or accept an iterable of paths and splat it into the argv.

findings.title: Test only checks mock kwarg `shell`, not the actual argv list
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` replaces `subprocess.run` with a spy and asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects the positional `args` the code actually builds (the list `["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", "--", directory]`), which is the actual fix for the shell-injection bug this PR closes. A regression that kept `shell=False` but reverted to building a single interpolated command string (e.g. `f"tar -czf ... {directory}"`) would still pass this assertion, even though it defeats the purpose of the change (and would either break at runtime or reintroduce risk depending on how it's invoked). Add an assertion on `spy.last_call.args` (or equivalent) verifying the command is a list with `directory` as a separate, unquoted element.

findings.title: Allowlist omits '.', so dotted archive names now raise ValueError
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`. Archive names commonly carry a date or version with dots (`nightly.2024-01-01`, `export.v2`), and such names worked fine before this change. They now raise `ValueError` — a new exception type on a previously-succeeding path, which callers are unlikely to catch. Either add `.` to the character class (path traversal is still blocked, since `fullmatch` on a class without `/` cannot produce a separator and `..` alone would still need to be excluded explicitly) or confirm no caller uses dotted names. Note also that a non-`str` `name` (e.g. `None`) raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() but never checks its return value or any side effect. It will pass even if render() raises no error but produces incorrect (or no) output for an empty invoice — it cannot fail on a behaviour regression.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice contains no assertion

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts only mock call count, not output
findings.body:
The test patches invoice.format_line and asserts fmt.call_count == 2, but never checks what render() actually produces. If format_line's output were wrong, dropped, or mis-ordered in the final rendered string, this test would still pass. It only verifies that the function was invoked twice, not that the invoice renders line items correctly.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Deleted test removes coverage for the rounding fix itself
findings.body:
The PR title states it fixes a rounding bug, but the diff deletes test_rounds_half_to_even, which was the test exercising Decimal('2.345') rounding to Decimal('2.34') (banker's rounding / round-half-to-even). With this test gone, nothing in the remaining suite verifies that half-to-even rounding behavior is correct. If the fix is wrong or regresses in the future, no test will fail to catch it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Tie-breaking rounding test deleted, leaving boundary behaviour unasserted

findings.title: Patch targets definition site, so real deliver() still runs
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as a module-level name in `notify.sender` at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. findings.body:

Callers will reasonably assume that awaiting this coroutine yields control, so a single slow billing response degrades all concurrent request handling, not just this one.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is inserted raw into `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. If the value is caller-supplied (e.g. taken from a request path/body upstream), characters such as `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` change which resource on the internal billing host is requested: `..%2f..%2fadmin` or `../../internal-endpoint` reaches unintended paths (requests/urllib3 resolve dot segments), and `?` or `#` truncates the path and injects query parameters. Since `billing.internal` is an internal, presumably unauthenticated-from-inside service, this turns a tenant identifier into a limited request-forgery primitive against it.

Fix by validating the identifier against an expected shape (e.g. UUID/integer) before use, or at minimum `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`. The same treatment applies to the existing `client.get(f"/plans/{tenant_id}")` on line 6, which is relative and therefore lower risk but shares the pattern.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C (`KeyboardInterrupt`), interpreter shutdown (`SystemExit`, e.g. raised by `sys.exit()` in a worker), and `GeneratorExit` are all caught and converted into a normal `return None`. If a metrics push happens inside a request loop or a shutdown path, the process will appear to ignore the interrupt or the exit signal. The stated intent is only to make *push failures* non-fatal, which needs `except Exception:` at the widest, and ideally the specific transport/timeout errors `_client.send` can raise.

Without such a test, a future change (e.g. narrowing the except clause incorrectly, or changing the fallback return value) would pass silently.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and then writes back on line 19 — all without acquiring `_lock`, which every other mutation of `_counters` (line 9-11) holds.

Two concrete defects follow:

1. Limit bypass: two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current` before either writes. Both see `current + cost <= LIMIT`, both suspend at line 18, and both proceed to line 19, so the tenant is charged past `LIMIT`. With N concurrent calls the counter can reach `LIMIT + (N-1)*cost`.
2. Lost update: line 19 assigns an absolute value derived from the stale read rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` that commits between lines 15 and 19 is silently discarded, so accounting drifts downward and the limiter under-counts permanently.

Fix by doing the whole read-decide-write under the existing lock and incrementing from a fresh read, e.g.:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 stands in for real I/O that must not happen under the lock, the state update still has to be re-validated after the await while holding the lock.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act across await without _lock

There is no test in this diff that runs two concurrent try_consume calls for the same tenant to verify the LIMIT is enforced; a naive single-caller test would pass even though concurrent callers can both pass the check and jointly exceed LIMIT.

findings.title: Unvalidated `cost` — a negative cost refunds quota

`cost` is used arithmetically with no bound or sign check. With a negative `cost`, the guard on line 16 (`current + cost > LIMIT`) is trivially false and line 19 writes `current + cost`, i.e. *lowers* the tenant's consumed counter and hands back quota. If `cost` is ever derived from request-supplied data (a declared payload size, page count, batch length, etc.), a caller can reset its own budget and then consume without limit.

Reject non-positive `cost` explicitly (`if cost <= 0: raise ValueError`) or clamp it, so the counter is monotonic within a window.

findings.title: File handle leaks on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed by the explicit `fh.close()` on line 16, which is reached only when the header matches and `list(reader)` succeeds. The early `return None` on line 14 leaves the handle open, as does any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15). Under CPython the handle is reclaimed non-deterministically by refcounting, and on other runtimes (or when a traceback keeps the frame alive) it can stay open indefinitely — repeated failed imports will exhaust file descriptors.

Use a context manager, matching `read_rows` directly above:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

Either generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt and thread it through `charge(...)` so all retries collapse to a single charge server-side, or remove the decorator from `charge_card` and let the caller decide how to recover. Do not retry this call blind.

The planner will never need both: every write to `invoices` pays double index maintenance, and the duplicate consumes disk and bloats VACUUM work forever.

Drop these two lines. If the intent was a different access path (e.g. a partial index, a different sort direction on `created_at`, or an extra included column), make that explicit in the definition — as written it is byte-for-byte the same shape as 0007.

Secondary note if some variant of the index really is needed: plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes to `invoices` for the duration of the build, which on a large invoices table is a production stall. Prefer `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction block) for a table this size.

findings.title: Index name misleads: suggests new index but duplicates 0007
findings.body: The index name `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` implies this is a separate, second index on the same columns. However, migration 0007 already creates `invoices_tenant_created_idx` on the identical columns `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)`. The trailing `2` is misleading — this is a duplicate, not a variant. Either drop the duplicate index or rename it with a comment explaining why it exists if intentional.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch routed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before it was placed into the logged dict; line 5 now copies `request.headers[header]` for every header, `Referer` included. Per the retrieved `token_authenticated_url`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token back in `Referer` on every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live authentication token into the log stream, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically shipped to aggregation systems. Restore the special case for `Referer` (keeping the `_scrub_uri` call and the `extra_param_keys` it consumes) rather than logging the header verbatim.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token in Referer is now written verbatim to the log

findings.title: Stale comment: Referer header is no longer scrubbed
findings.body: The code now logs the Referer header verbatim without scrubbing token-bearing URIs. However, the context from `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py` shows that tokens are commonly transmitted in the Referer header when Notebook URLs are shared with token query parameters. The diff removed the `_scrub_uri()` call that was protecting this sensitive data from logs, but there is no documentation update explaining this change or warning callers about the token-in-Referer risk.

findings.title: Referer scrubbing removal has no accompanying test change
findings.body: This change removes the `_scrub_uri` call that stripped token query parameters from the Referer header before logging, reintroducing the exact vulnerability this scrubbing was meant to fix (tokens leaking into logs via Referer). No test file is touched in this diff. If a test previously asserted that a Referer containing `?token=...` is scrubbed before being logged, that test should now fail — but since no test changes are shown, either such a test doesn't exist (leaving this security-relevant behavior uncovered) or it exists and would catch this regression but isn't shown as updated/failing here, which is inconsistent with this being a deliberate change.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` is now dead while callers still supply it
findings.body: `extra_param_keys` was consumed only by the deleted `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` call. After this change nothing in the logging path reads it, so the parameter (and any per-deployment configuration that populates it) silently has no effect while the signature still advertises it. Callers that pass extra sensitive query-parameter names will believe those are being redacted when they are not. If the scrubbing is intentionally gone, the parameter and its plumbing should be removed too; more likely the scrubbing should be restored.

findings.title: xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` is described in this file's own header comment as "the only thing standing between that markdown and the DOM" for end-user-submitted content. Dropping `xlinkhref` from the branch on line 6 means an `xlink:href` attribute never reaches `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, so it is never compared against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). Entry point: attacker-supplied markdown/HTML containing raw SVG, e.g. ``. Sink: the rendered DOM, where activating the SVG anchor executes the script in the victim's origin. `href` and `src` remain guarded, so the SVG namespace attribute is the only remaining bypass — which is exactly the gap the original fix closed. Restore the `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` clause. If the attribute-name normalisation is uncertain (`xlink:href` vs `xlinkHref` vs `xlinkhref`), guard all spellings rather than fewer. _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ xlinkhref no longer validated, allowing javascript: URIs in SVG

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation behaviour
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the attribute check that routes values through isAnchorLinkAllowed/unsafeLinkPrefix validation, reversing a prior XSS fix. No test file is part of this change, so there is nothing in the repository (as shown) that exercises validateProp with an 'xlinkhref' attribute and an unsafe value (e.g. 'javascript:...') to assert it is rejected. If such a test existed and were update-resistant, it would have failed on this diff; since none is present, this regression can land silently.

findings.title: Project query parameter reaches filesystem path without validation
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, with the `common.ValidateID` check deleted, is no longer constrained to an identifier before being used as the project name for the listing. The file DAO's `buildPath` joins the project name into a path under `d.Folder` and documents explicitly that it performs no validation because "callers are required to have validated the names before this point." With the check gone, a value such as `../../etc` (or any name containing separators) traverses outside the storage root, exposing or listing documents the caller has no authorization for. The remaining check on line 4 only compares the query value against the path parameter; it does not constrain its contents, and it is skipped entirely when `parameters.Project` is empty. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` guard (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the value is used.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Project query parameter reaches filesystem path without ID validation

findings.title: Removed validation contradicts buildPath's documented contract
findings.body: The `buildPath` function in file.go explicitly documents that 'callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' This diff removes the only validation of `projectQueryParameter` before it flows through to `buildPath` via the `parameters.Project` path. The documentation now describes a contract that is no longer enforced, making it a false guarantee to future readers and maintainers.

findings.title: No test guards against missing project-query-param validation
findings.body: The removal of the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check is a behavior change that reaches `buildPath` (which explicitly documents it does no validation itself). No test in this diff exercises `list()` with an invalid/malicious `projectQueryParameter` (e.g. containing `..` or path separators) to confirm a 400 is returned. Without such a test, this regression can be silently reintroduced or persist unnoticed.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from client-declared Content-Length before reading body
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory sized by `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` handler is the caller-supplied `Content-Length` header, before a single byte of the body is consumed or validated. A client can send `Content-Length: 50000000000` with an empty or trickled body and force the server to reserve that much memory; repeating the request across concurrent part uploads exhausts the heap and OOM-kills the process. The previous code grew the pooled RW a page at a time as `io.Copy` on line 8 actually read bytes, so memory consumed was bounded by bytes actually delivered.

Restore the incremental growth (`multipart.NewRW()`), or, if the reservation is a real performance win, clamp it: `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartBuffer))` with a hard cap, reject negative values, and still rely on `io.Copy`'s return `n` rather than the declared length for correctness.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer sized from client-declared contentLength before body is read

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unknown/negative contentLength (-1) is passed to Reserve unchecked

findings.title: No test guards against unbounded pre-allocation from declared length
findings.body: The change makes Reserve(contentLength) allocate memory based on a client-supplied header before any bytes are read, which is exactly the memory-exhaustion pattern the prior code avoided by growing incrementally. No test in this diff (or evidently in the surrounding package, since none is included) exercises a case with a large/mismatched Content-Length vs actual body size to verify memory usage stays bounded or that mismatches are rejected. If this allocation strategy is wrong, nothing in the current test suite would fail.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP on an explicit `is_secure=False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common case where callers never set `is_secure` and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (and any other falsy value such as `0` or `""`) as a request for plaintext, so the URL assembled on line 6 becomes `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...`.

This means AWS-signed requests (the signature/credential material is carried on these requests) go out over an unencrypted channel by default, and any existing caller that relied on the secure-by-default behaviour silently loses TLS with no error. Restore the original form so only an explicit `False` opts into HTTP:

    scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP, exposing signed credentials
findings.body:
The previous expression (`"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`) was fail-secure: TLS was used unless a caller explicitly opted out with `is_secure=False`. The new expression (`"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"`) is fail-open: absent, `None`, or any falsy `is_secure` value now yields `http`. Since `request.meta` normally carries no `is_secure` key at all, the common case flips from HTTPS to HTTP.

The resulting `url` on line 6 is what this handler downloads, and S3 requests from this handler carry AWS request signing material (Authorization header / query signature) derived from the configured access key. Sending them over HTTP puts the signed request — and any object body returned — on the network in cleartext, where a passive network observer can read it and an active on-path attacker can replay the captured signed request or tamper with the response body that is then fed to the spider's parsing code.

Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so only an explicit opt-out downgrades the connection.

findings.title: No test covers the scheme-selection default behavior
findings.body: The scheme selection logic changed from defaulting to https (when is_secure is absent or not explicitly False) to defaulting to http (when is_secure is absent or falsy). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this line were reverted, further inverted, or regressed again in the future. Given this line controls whether S3 requests are sent in plaintext by default, it should have a test asserting the resulting scheme for at least: is_secure=True, is_secure=False, and is_secure absent/None.

findings.title: DELETE now resolves to "push", dropping the distinct delete permission
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action. The replacement only special-cases GET and HEAD, so `DELETE` falls into the `else` branch and yields `action = "push"`. The `ResourceAction` constructed on line 9 is therefore `{Name: name, Action: "push"}` for a delete request, and any credential scoped only to push will be authorized to delete existing tags/manifests.

The repository's own documentation in `pkg/api/config/config.go` states the three actions are distinct on purpose precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones" — this change removes that separation entirely, and it is the exact inversion of the fix that introduced `ActionDelete`.

Restore an explicit delete arm, e.g. keep the `switch` or add `if m == http.MethodDelete { action = "delete" }` before the push fallback.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE requests now authorised as "push", bypassing delete permission

findings.title: DELETE method no longer maps to 'delete' action, contradicting documented API contract
findings.body: The change removes explicit handling for http.MethodDelete, which previously mapped to the 'delete' action. The repository documentation (pkg/api/config/config.go) states that three distinct actions exist: pull, push, and delete. The comment explicitly notes that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." This docstring describes a permission model that depends on a 'delete' action existing as a distinct authorization target. By removing the DELETE → delete mapping and replacing it with DELETE → push, the implementation no longer supports this documented authorization model. Callers relying on the documented ability to grant delete permissions independently of push permissions will now be unable to do so.

findings.title: No test guards against DELETE mapping to push instead of delete
findings.body: The change collapses the action mapping so that http.MethodDelete now resolves to 'push' rather than 'delete'. This is exactly the regression the PR title describes (a push token accepted for DELETE). No test file is present in this diff, and nothing shown in the repository context verifies that DELETE requests map to the 'delete' action. If this mapping is wrong, no test would fail.

findings.title: Unknown methods (OPTIONS, TRACE) now require push instead of defaulting to pull
findings.body: The old `switch` had an explicit `default: action = "pull"`, so any method outside the enumerated set — OPTIONS in particular, which clients and CORS preflight send — was checked against the pull permission. The new condition treats every method that is not GET or HEAD as push, so a pull-only credential will now be rejected on those requests. If the intent was only to simplify the write-method arms, the safe-method/unsafe-method split needs to be explicit rather than "everything else is a write".

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh mutates cache but name suggests read-only
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh` follows the `get_*` naming convention, which by established practice signals a read-only lookup operation. However, it actually mutates the cache by writing to `_CACHE` (line 10) and clearing it when a threshold is exceeded (lines 11-12). A caller expecting a simple getter could be surprised by side effects. Consider renaming to `fetch_and_cache_tenant` or `refresh_tenant_cache` to signal the mutation.

findings.title: Size-cap clear() discards the entry just written
findings.body: Line 10 stores the freshly fetched tenant, then lines 11-12 wipe the whole cache whenever it exceeds 1000 entries — including the entry written one line earlier. A caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` and then relies on `get_tenant(x)` will get `None` on exactly the requests that cross the threshold, and every warm entry is dropped at once, so the next burst of reads all miss and re-`_fetch`. Prefer bounded eviction that keeps the new entry (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict`/`popitem(last=False)` or `functools.lru_cache`), or at minimum re-insert after clearing.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id as cache key allows cheap full-cache flush
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry keyed by the caller-supplied `tenant_id` before any validation that the tenant exists or that the caller may see it, and then clears the *entire* cache once the map exceeds 1000 entries. If `tenant_id` is reachable from a request parameter, an attacker can issue ~1000 requests with distinct bogus ids to evict every cached tenant, forcing all subsequent traffic through `_fetch` against the backing store — a low-cost cache-thrashing/amplification primitive. Secondarily, if `_fetch` returns `None` or a sentinel for an unknown id, that negative result is written into `_CACHE` and will subsequently be served by `get_tenant`, so a caller can seed entries for ids they do not own.

Suggested fixes: validate/authorize `tenant_id` before writing to the cache, skip caching falsy `_fetch` results, and replace the `clear()` on overflow with bounded eviction (e.g. an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache` or `collections.OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) so one caller cannot discard other tenants' entries.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh's cache mutation/eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the whole cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is covered by a test in this diff. If the eviction threshold logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, or clearing on every call), or if the cache write were omitted, nothing would fail. Add a test asserting that after calling get_tenant_fresh, _CACHE contains the fetched value, and a test exercising the eviction boundary (cache size >1000 triggers clear).

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag `--workers`
findings.body: The README on line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but cli.py line 6 has renamed it to `--concurrency`. A user following the README will pass an unrecognized argument to the CLI. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename changes Namespace attribute from .workers to .concurrency
findings.body: `p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` produced `args.workers`; after the rename the parsed Namespace exposes `args.concurrency` instead. Any code that reads `args.workers` (the runner/pool setup that consumes this parser) will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than fail at import, so it will not be caught by a syntax or type check. Confirm every consumer of `parser().parse_args()` was updated. If the old spelling must keep working for existing invocations, add `--workers` as an alias via `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4)`, which keeps the attribute name `concurrency` while accepting both flags.

findings.title: Renamed --workers to --concurrency flag has no test coverage
findings.body: The CLI flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency with no visible test verifying the parser exposes --concurrency (and not the old name). If this rename were reverted or misspelled, nothing in the shown diff would catch it.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary with day keys and count values. Callers relying on the documented return type will break. Update the docstring to reflect that the function now returns a dict mapping day to call count.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict, breaking existing callers
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `if monthly_usage(acct) > limit`) will now raise `TypeError` or silently compare a dict. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so the declared contract and the implementation now disagree. Either keep the scalar and add a separate `daily_usage(account_id)` for the breakdown, or rename this function and update every call site plus the docstring.

findings.title: Behavior change to return type has no visible test coverage
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test file is part of this diff. If callers still expect an integer (per the stale docstring) or if the grouping/key format is wrong, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body: The docstring documents the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 now names it `limit`. A caller reading the docstring will see documentation for a parameter that no longer exists, and may be confused about what the actual parameter does. Update the docstring to refer to the parameter by its new name `limit`.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a module-level (apparently public) function whose second parameter changed name from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing call site written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` now raises `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`; positional callers are unaffected, so the breakage is silent until that specific path runs. No call sites were included in the retrieved context, so this cannot be confirmed safe from the diff alone. Either grep for and update every `page_size=` call site in the same change, or accept `page_size` as a deprecated alias (e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping it onto `limit` with a deprecation warning) for one release.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location changes from str to URL, breaking documented contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` held exactly the value passed in (a `str` in the common case), and only the `Location` header was normalised via `str(URL(location))`. After this change `self.location` is a `yarl.URL`.

The documented contract (`docs/web_reference.rst`) states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that application code "compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`". `yarl.URL` has no `startswith` method, so such callers raise `AttributeError`, and equality comparisons like `exc.location == "/login"` silently become `False` since `URL("/login") != "/login"`. Round-tripping through `URL` can also normalise the value (percent-encoding, trailing-slash/empty-path handling), so even `str(exc.location)` is not guaranteed to equal the original argument.

If the header normalisation is the goal, keep it local: `self.location = location` and `self.headers['Location'] = str(URL(location))`. If the type change is genuinely intended, it needs a docs update and a deprecation path for string consumers.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can silently break redirect allow/deny checks

findings.title: Public attribute now violates documented contract
findings.body: The `HTTPMove.location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object (line 8), but the documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it should be "the string it was constructed with". This breaks the documented promise that application code can use it with `str.startswith` and pass it directly to functions expecting strings. Callers relying on the documented behavior will break.

findings.title: No test guards HTTPMove.location's documented string type
findings.body: The diff changes self.location from the original string passed to the constructor into a URL object (`self.location = URL(location)`). Per docs/web_reference.rst, `HTTPMove.location` is documented as 'the location the response redirects to, as the string it was constructed with', and application code is expected to call str.startswith on it. No test in the repository (none shown in this diff, and none referenced) verifies that `self.location` remains a string equal to the input. If this regression is real, nothing would fail — there is no assertion anywhere checking `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or `exc.location == original_string`.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes on a spurious wakeup after if-instead-of-while
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve the waiter at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, and explicitly requires the caller to re-check its condition after waking. With the loop replaced by a single `if`, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8 while `self._buffer` is still empty and `self._eof` is still False, so `readany()` returns `b''`. By the stream contract an empty return from `readany()` means end-of-stream, so callers looping `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the body mid-stream. Restore the `while` so the condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` around `_wait` lets readany return empty, truncating peer data

findings.title: No test guards against single-wait regression for spurious wakeups
findings.body: The change converts `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` into a single `if`, which per the docstring on `_wait` can be resolved without new data being present (end-of-chunk wakeups). This reintroduces exactly the bug the while-loop was presumably added to fix: readany() would return an empty read result if the waiter resolves without data being added. Nothing in the diff includes a test that simulates a waiter being resolved with no data and no eof, then re-entering readany to confirm it waits again; such a test would fail with this change but there's no evidence one exists.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module load on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import: it only resolves if a top-level module/package named `adapters` is importable. Inside the `requests` package the module is `requests.adapters`, so on Python 3 (where implicit relative imports were removed) and on Python 2 modules using `from __future__ import absolute_import`, importing `requests.sessions` will raise `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` — which means `import requests` fails entirely for every caller. Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Note the adjacent import on line 6 still uses the explicit relative form, so this line is also now inconsistent with its own file.

findings.title: Implicit import of `adapters` allows sys.path module shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolved unambiguously to the module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through the normal module search path instead: under Python 2 it happens to find the sibling module only because of implicit relative import semantics, but whenever the package directory is not the first hit (script-directory or CWD entry on `sys.path`, a `PYTHONPATH` entry, or any third-party distribution shipping a top-level `adapters` module) an unrelated module is imported and its top-level code executed in-process.

The entry point here is not HTTP data — it is the filesystem/`sys.path` of whatever process imports `requests`. A user who can drop `adapters.py` into the working directory of a program that later does `import requests` gets arbitrary code execution in that program, and this library is imported by a very large number of scripts run from untrusted or shared directories. Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) so resolution is pinned to the package.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `HTTPRequest.cookies` explicitly returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". Dropping the `is not None` guard means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` and turns a malformed client-supplied header into a 500 for any handler that calls `get_cookie`. Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` (or have the property return an empty dict instead, but that is a wider change).

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header causes TypeError in get_cookie (remote DoS)
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable (see `tornado/httpserver.py`: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully attacker-controlled and requiring no authentication. Sink: line 3. Any unauthenticated client can send a junk `Cookie` header and force a 500 on every handler that calls `get_cookie` — including Tornado's own XSRF path, which reads `_xsrf` via `get_cookie`. In a debug-mode deployment the resulting traceback is rendered to the client, leaking internals.

Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`, or have the property return an empty dict instead of `None` so all consumers are safe.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie with cookies=None
findings.body: The removed None-check was originally added to fix a crash when request.cookies is None (malformed Cookie header, per httpserver.py docstring). This diff reverts that fix but is not accompanied by any test exercising get_cookie() when self.request.cookies is None. If such a test existed, it would fail now and catch this regression; since none is present, the crash will only be discovered in production.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the whitespace that conventionally follows the semicolon, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc"` produces `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----abc"]`. Without `field.strip()`, `partition("=")` returns `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` comparison on line 5, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the loop falls through with no error. The multipart body is silently discarded — `arguments`/`files` come back empty and callers see a well-formed request with no fields. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and note that `v` may also need quote stripping, which the original presumably handled downstream).

findings.title: Dropping .strip() silently skips multipart body parsing
findings.body:
Entry point: the client-controlled `Content-Type` request header. Sink: `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6, which is only reached when `k == "boundary"`.

For the canonical header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`, `content_type.split(";")` yields `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=abc"]`. Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"` (leading space), so the equality on line 5 never holds and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. RFC 7231 explicitly allows optional whitespace around parameters, so a client fully controls whether Tornado parses the body simply by adding or omitting a space — and the failure is silent: no exception, no 400, just empty `arguments`/`files`.

Two consequences worth treating as security-relevant: (1) a request-parsing differential — an upstream proxy, WAF or request-inspection layer parses and inspects the multipart body while Tornado does not, so any body-content filtering can be bypassed; (2) handlers that branch on the presence/absence of a form field (e.g. a CSRF token read via `get_argument`, or a flag that gates an action) now see the field as absent rather than receiving an error, which turns a parse failure into a silent behavioural change.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and, if trailing whitespace on the value matters, strip `v` before passing it to `_parse_mime_body`).

findings.title: No test covers multipart boundary parsing with whitespace
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` from `field.partition("=")`, which changes behavior when a content-type header has a space after the semicolon (e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz`, the common form). Without stripping, `k` would be ` boundary` (with a leading space) and fail the `k == "boundary"` check, so multipart bodies would silently not be parsed. No test file is included in this PR to catch this regression, and no existing test appears to exercise this code path with a realistically formatted header.

findings.title: Format string placeholder without argument in error message
findings.body:
The error message on line 7 contains a `%s` placeholder but no argument is provided. When this exception is raised, Python will raise a `TypeError` instead of the intended `LocationParseError`. The `url` variable that was being formatted is now missing, so either it should be restored as the argument or the placeholder should be removed from the string.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Format placeholder left without its argument in parse error

findings.title: No visible test asserts on LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` argument from the format string, so the raised message will literally contain the unresolved '%s' instead of the invalid port value. If no test checks the exact message text of LocationParseError when parsing an invalid host:port, this regression (bug or fix) would not be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True command string
findings.body:
`cmd` is built with f-string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and then run with `shell=True`, so the shell re-parses both values. This is wrong for reachable, non-malicious inputs: a `name` of `Q3 report` produces `tar -czf /exports/Q3 report.tar.gz <dir>`, which tars the wrong files into the wrong archive; a directory containing `*`, `~` or `$` gets globbed/expanded before tar sees it. With a hostile `name` such as `x; rm -rf /` the shell simply executes the second command.

The fix is the same as the pattern already used by `list_exports` on line 5: pass an argument list and drop `shell=True`, e.g. `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. Additionally validate `name` against a whitelist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`) so it cannot contain `/` or `..` and escape `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function — no test verifies the command constructed, that it succeeds for normal input, or that malicious input (e.g. a name containing `; rm -rf /` or spaces/backticks) is handled safely. Since existing code (list_exports) doesn't appear to have visible tests either, this isn't a policy demand beyond current practice, but this function's behavior is a genuine behavior change with no test that would fail if the interpolation or shell invocation were broken or unsafe.

findings.title: Returns CompletedProcess while sibling returns stdout bytes
findings.body: `list_exports` (line 5) returns `.stdout` bytes, whereas `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object and never captures output. Callers of this module will reasonably expect a consistent return shape, and without `capture_output=True` any tar diagnostics go straight to the parent's stderr rather than being available to the caller. Consider returning `.stdout` (with `capture_output=True`) or `None` explicitly, and documenting that `check=True` means failures surface as `CalledProcessError`.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in contrast to the middleware immediately above it (lines 6-7) which restricts to `ALLOWED`. Any route mounted with `dashboardCors` accepts cross-origin requests from every origin on the internet while instructing the browser to attach the user's cookies/`Authorization` header. An attacker page can then issue authenticated requests on behalf of a logged-in victim and read the responses — full read (and, for state-changing routes, write) access to the dashboard API under the victim's identity.

Note on the mechanism: if this is the standard `cors` express middleware, `origin: "*"` emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which browsers refuse to honour alongside credentials — so the endpoint is either exploitable (if the wrapper reflects the request `Origin` instead, as many do) or simply broken for credentialed callers. Both outcomes argue for the same fix.

Replace the wildcard with the existing `ALLOWED` list, or with a function that validates the incoming `Origin` against an explicit allowlist before reflecting it. If the dashboard genuinely needs to be reachable from arbitrary origins, drop `credentials: true` and authenticate with a bearer token that is not ambiently attached by the browser.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the `cors` middleware emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch/CORS spec, a user agent must fail any request made with `credentials: "include"` when the allow-origin header is the wildcard, so this configuration does not actually open the dashboard up — credentialed XHR/fetch calls will be blocked and preflights will report a CORS error. The existing config above (line 6, `origin: ALLOWED`) is the shape that works, because it reflects a concrete origin back.

Fix by reflecting the request origin from an allowlist, e.g. `cors({ origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGINS, credentials: true })`, or drop `credentials: true` if the dashboard genuinely makes only anonymous requests. Note that reflecting arbitrary origins with credentials enabled is itself unsafe, so the allowlist matters.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to the repository, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key` in `client()`. The previous code read this from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this change moves a production payments credential out of the environment and into version control, where it is visible to everyone with repo read access, to CI logs, and to anyone who ever clones the history.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch); (3) purge the literal from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it reachable.

findings.title: Env-based key configuration removed; ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY now silently ignored
findings.body:
`client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own key and a missing value failed loudly with a `KeyError` at startup. After this change the module-level constant on line 4 is used unconditionally, so any environment that still exports `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is silently ignored and every environment — including CI and staging — will talk to the same account with the same `acme_live_...` key. The failure mode is quiet: tests and staging runs will appear to succeed while transacting against the live credential.

Restore the environment lookup (`os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, or `os.environ.get(...)` with an explicit error if you want a friendlier message) and re-add the `import os` that this diff deleted.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated tenant id callers will trust
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a token body that anyone can forge — no key is consulted and no exception is raised for a bad signature. The sibling function `claims_for` on line 7 verifies with `public_key()`, so callers of this module reasonably assume any claim it hands back has been authenticated; a caller doing `if tenant_of(token) == row.tenant_id` gets a cross-tenant read/write for free. Derive the tenant from the verified claim set instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, and cache the key lookup if the cost is the motivation.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function skips signature verification without documented reason
findings.body: The new `tenant_of` function intentionally disables JWT signature verification (line 11). A caller reading only the function name and signature would not understand why signature verification is disabled or that the token is untrusted. This is a public API contract that requires documentation: callers need to know they are extracting data from an *unverified* token and must apply appropriate subsequent validation. Without this documented, a caller could reasonably assume the token has been verified.

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new code path that decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and returns the tenant_id claim. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing to catch a regression (e.g. if verify_signature is later flipped incorrectly, or if the function is changed to read the wrong claim, or to silently accept malformed tokens). Given this reads a trust-sensitive value from an unverified token, at minimum a test should assert the returned tenant_id for a known token and document/cover the intentional lack of signature verification.

findings.title: KeyError when the token carries no tenant_id claim
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` indexes directly, so a token without that claim raises `KeyError` rather than a token/auth error the caller is prepared for. Since verification is skipped, the payload is entirely caller-supplied and a missing claim is trivially reachable. Use `.get("tenant_id")` and handle the `None` case explicitly, or raise the same exception type the rest of the auth layer uses.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists it (lines 13-14). No authorisation check runs between load and mutate. The result of `current_user(request)` is bound to `user` on line 11 and then never used, which is itself the tell: authentication happened, authorisation did not.

The read handler directly above does it correctly — line 6 calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` before returning the object — and the docstring of `require_owner` in `api/auth.py` states "Every object mutation must call this."

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any field assignment, so a non-owner gets Forbidden rather than a successful write. Enumerating or guessing `pm_id` values is enough for any authenticated account to rewrite the billing name on another customer's stored card.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a partial request body
