findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner(user, pm), unlike the neighboring get endpoint which does call it (line 6). This is a behavior change (new authorization-sensitive endpoint) with no accompanying test in the diff. A test asserting that a non-owner request to update_payment_method raises Forbidden would have caught this; since no such test exists, nothing currently fails when this authorization gap is introduced or later regresses.

findings.title: Public API endpoint lacks docstring and authorization documentation
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint that takes a user-controlled `pm_id` parameter and mutates a PaymentMethod object, but has no docstring. A caller reading only the function signature would not know (1) that it checks authorization, (2) what fields can be updated, or (3) what errors it raises. The repository's own `auth.py` states 'Every object mutation must call this' referring to `require_owner`, but this function does not call it, making the contract actively misleading about what access control applies.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` was previously protected by `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its import are deleted, so the handler now accepts unlimited calls. The `email` parameter comes straight from the request and flows into `send_reset_email(email)` with no throttle in between. Consequences: (1) mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, (2) burning reset-token quota / SMTP reputation, (3) if the response or timing differs for known vs unknown addresses, cheap account enumeration, and (4) if reset tokens are short-lived but guessable, high-volume issuance widens the guessing window. Restore the decorator, or move the limit to a middleware/gateway layer and say so explicitly in the change. A per-email limit plus a per-source-IP limit is the usual pairing.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of rate limiting
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`. Nothing in this diff (no test file present) verifies that repeated calls to `request_reset` are throttled, so this regression—and any future reintroduction of it—would go undetected by the test suite. Add a test that calls `request_reset` more than the allowed threshold and asserts subsequent calls are rejected/limited.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` joins the caller-supplied `name` straight onto `EXPORT_ROOT` and opens the result. `os.path.join` does not confine: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside the export root, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. The function immediately above (line 14) runs the same untrusted input through `_confined(name)` first, which is evidently the intended normalise-and-confine step. Route this function through `_confined(name)` too rather than reimplementing the join.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks documented API contract
findings.body: The `read_export_preview` function is exported at module level and has a different security contract than the existing `read_export` function: it does not use the `_confined()` path normalization that the sibling function uses. A caller reading the first function's pattern and applying it to the second would expect the same confinement to apply, but it does not. This difference must be documented in a docstring explaining why path confinement is skipped here, or the inconsistency itself indicates a bug. At minimum, the function needs a docstring that explains its parameters and security properties.

findings.title: No test covers read_export_preview's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview joins EXPORT_ROOT with an unvalidated name and never calls the _confined() normalisation used by the neighboring handler. There is no test in this diff exercising this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret') to confirm it is either confined or intentionally unconfined. Since the sibling function's confinement behavior is presumably tested, this new function's divergent behavior would go unnoticed by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export: cross-tenant data read
findings.body:
`bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` by raw ID from the request and returns it serialized, with no tenant check in between. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced `report.tenant_id == user.tenant_id` was deleted along with its import, and `user` is now computed on line 5 but never used \u2014 a direct signal that the only consumer of the identity was the authorization check. Any caller who can guess or enumerate report IDs now receives another tenant's report bodies in full.

If the loop is the performance problem, keep the control and make it cheap: filter at the query layer instead, e.g. fetch with `Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and raise `Forbidden` if the returned count differs from `len(report_ids)`. Do not merge this as written.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export — cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: No test guards ownership enforcement in bulk_export
findings.body: The removal of the require_owner loop means bulk_export now returns reports regardless of tenant ownership. There is no test in this diff (or evident in the repo context) that calls bulk_export with a report belonging to a different tenant and asserts Forbidden is raised. If such a test existed and were passing before, this change should have broken it, but no test file is touched here, meaning the regression is currently invisible to CI. Add a test that asserts Forbidden (or equivalent) is raised when a user requests a report outside their tenant.

findings.title: Public endpoint documentation contradicts removed auth check
findings.body: The bulk_export function is a public endpoint that reads Report objects belonging to potentially different tenants, but the require_owner check has been removed. The docstring in api/auth.py explicitly states that "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this [require_owner]". Either the docstring must be updated to reflect the new architectural decision, or the requirement must be documented at the endpoint level so callers understand the authorization contract. A caller reading the auth.py documentation would reasonably expect all cross-tenant reads to be guarded, but this endpoint violates that contract without documented explanation.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract, breaking on quoted input
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling function `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead builds the full statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with `params=None`.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly incorrect for reachable inputs: a search term such as `O'Brien` closes the quoted literal and makes the statement a syntax error, a term containing `%` or `_` silently changes LIKE matching semantics, and `None` for either argument is stringified into the literal `'None'` rather than producing an IS NULL / no-op condition.

Fix by keeping every value in `params`, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, letting the driver quote and escape both values.

findings.title: No test coverage for new search_customers function
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL via an f-string with unescaped user input (term, status) instead of using parameterised queries like get_customer. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so neither the injection behavior nor a future fix to use proper parameterisation would be caught by any test.

findings.title: Public function `search_customers` lacks parameter documentation
findings.body: The function `search_customers` is a public API exported from the queries module. It accepts two parameters (`term` and `status`) but provides no docstring explaining what they represent, their expected types, or how they are used. A caller reading only the signature could not determine the function's behaviour or constraints.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary caller-supplied URL
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight into `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it in the same module resolves the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before calling `requests.post`, so the module already establishes that these URLs are untrusted and that an allowlist is the intended control — the new entry point simply does not apply it.

Consequences if `url` comes from customer input (the PR title says customers register a webhook target): an attacker can make the server issue GETs to internal-only addresses — `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` on EC2, `http://metadata.google.internal/`, `127.0.0.1`/`10.0.0.0/8` admin panels — and learn from the returned status code whether each target exists, giving an internal port/host scanner and potentially credential access via metadata services. Non-HTTP schemes are also unblocked (`file://` is rejected by requests, but `http+unix`/custom adapters and redirect chains are not).

Fix: route this through the same validation as the send path — parse the URL, require scheme in `{https}` (or `{http, https}`), resolve the host and check it against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` *and* against private/link-local/loopback ranges, and pass `allow_redirects=False` (requests follows redirects by default, so an allowlisted host can 302 to `169.254.169.254` and defeat a host check applied only to the initial URL). Extracting the existing check into a shared `_assert_allowed(url)` helper called by both functions is the smallest correct change.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check its sibling enforces

findings.title: verify_endpoint lacks any test and skips the allowlist check used elsewhere
findings.body: verify_endpoint(url) performs a live GET request against an arbitrary caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before making a request. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing exercises this new function's behavior (e.g. that it should reject disallowed hosts, or that it correctly returns a status code). If this function were later changed to be more permissive, or if it is used somewhere that assumes it also validates the host, nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` on `acme-customer-invoices`. These settings are the account-independent backstop that prevents a public ACL or bucket policy — applied by anyone with `s3:PutBucketAcl`/`s3:PutBucketPolicy`, or by a mistake in a later commit — from actually exposing objects. With them off, a single public-read ACL or a `Principal: "*"` policy immediately makes customer invoices world-readable, and `ignore_public_acls = false` means even per-object public ACLs take effect.

The PR description states this bucket is not meant to be public, so this looks like the block from the `assets` bucket copy-pasted. Set all four to `true` for the invoices bucket (or drop the resource entirely and rely on the S3 default, which blocks public access).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all four public access block protections

findings.title: Invoices bucket public access lacks documentation
findings.body: The invoices bucket (lines 13-23) is configured identically to the assets bucket with all public access blocks disabled (block_public_acls, block_public_policy, ignore_public_acls, restrict_public_buckets all set to false), making it publicly readable and writable. However, there is no comment explaining whether this public configuration is intentional. The assets bucket's public access is described in the PR title as deliberate ("One bucket is deliberately public"), but invoices containing customer financial data should typically be private. Without documentation clarifying intent, a future operator cannot distinguish between a correct configuration and a misconfiguration.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex-digest HMAC as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison leaks how many leading characters of the expected signature the attacker guessed correctly. Because the attacker controls `header` and can replay the same body arbitrarily many times, this is the standard byte-at-a-time forgery oracle against a webhook signature — the effective work drops from brute-forcing a 256-bit digest to a few thousand requests per hex character. Replace with `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the sibling function on line 7. (Note the two are not exactly behaviourally equivalent either: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a `None`/non-ASCII-str `header` where `==` quietly returns `False`, so if callers can pass a missing header, guard for it explicitly rather than relying on `==`.)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test exercises verify_acmepay's comparison behavior
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new public function with security-relevant behavior (signature verification) and no accompanying test in this diff. Since no test file is present, nothing would catch a regression or the difference in comparison semantics versus verify_stripe.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned to client
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now returns `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` in the HTTP 500 response. Any client that can provoke an unhandled exception — malformed input, a bad path parameter, a DB timeout — receives absolute file paths, module and function names, source line fragments, library versions, and frequently the offending values themselves (e.g. a failed SQL statement or a connection string embedded in a driver error). That is a free map of the deployment for anyone probing the service, and driver/ORM exceptions have a real habit of carrying credentials in their message text.

Keep the client-facing body opaque and keep the detail server-side, where `log.exception` on line 8 already captures the full traceback. If developers need the detail returned inline, gate it on an explicit debug/non-production flag rather than making it the default, and consider returning a correlation ID the client can quote instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    request_id = new_request_id()
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"request_id": request_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": request_id}, 500
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores `exc` and reads ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body is no longer stable: new key and variable `error` value

findings.title: No test guards against leaking exception/traceback to client
findings.body: The `handle` function now returns the raw exception string and full traceback in the response body. There is no test file in this diff verifying the response shape, so nothing would fail if this were reverted to a safe error message, and nothing would catch a future accidental widening of what gets leaked (e.g., swapping in a different exception type with sensitive data in its message).

findings.title: Reset path produces MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body:
`hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`) which can only be checked with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest with no salt and no cost factor. If the reset flow writes this value into the same stored-password column, either (a) login verification via `bcrypt.checkpw` will reject it and the reset silently produces an unusable account, or (b) the verification code has a fallback branch that compares MD5, in which case every password set through reset is stored unsalted and brute-forceable at billions of guesses per second. Both outcomes are defects; they differ only in which one you get.

Make the reset path call `hash_password` (or bcrypt directly) so the stored format is uniform, and if any MD5 values have already been written, force a rehash on next successful login.

findings.title: Password reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted MD5 pass, while `hash_password` on line 7 uses bcrypt with a per-password salt. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no salt here, so any dump of these values is trivially reversible for common passwords via rainbow tables or brute force, and identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts.

Use the same primitive as the primary path: `return bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode()` — or simply delete this function and call `hash_password`. Note also that values written by this function will not verify against `bcrypt.checkpw`, so if both paths write to the same credential column the reset flow either breaks login or forces a weaker verification branch elsewhere; both outcomes are worth checking.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot name the HTTP entry point that feeds `raw`; the sink (the stored digest) is nonetheless clear from the function name and its sibling.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing and checksum logic have no tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are new, behaviorally distinct functions (hashing scheme selection, file I/O handling) introduced in this diff, but no test file is included in the change. There is no repository context shown indicating existing coverage for auth/passwords.py, so this appears to be a genuine gap: a regression in either function's output or a change in the hashing/reading logic would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled script with repo secrets
findings.body:
This change makes the workflow trigger on `pull_request_target` (line 4), which runs in the context of the base repository with access to repository secrets and a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and is not gated behind maintainer approval for first-time contributors. Line 12 then explicitly checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the fork's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on line 15.

Entry point: any unprivileged user opens a pull request from a fork containing an edited `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, plus package manifests/lockfiles with install hooks, if the script runs a package manager). Sink: `run:` shell execution on line 13, with `NPM_TOKEN` readable via `env` and the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` readable from the runner environment/`.git/config` left by `actions/checkout`. The attacker can exfiltrate the npm token (publish rights) and, depending on default permissions, push to the base repository.

Remediation options, in order of preference:
- Revert to `pull_request`. A size measurement does not need secrets or base-repo write access; if `NPM_TOKEN` is only needed for an authenticated registry read, consider whether the measurement can work without it.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but its body contains no `await` — it calls `requests.get`, which is a synchronous, blocking I/O call. Inside an event loop this blocks the entire loop thread for the full duration of the request, up to the 5 second timeout, stalling every other concurrent task in the process (including the awaited `client.get` on line 6 that callers run alongside it). Under load this serialises all request handling behind the slowest billing call.

Use the async client already imported in this module, mirroring `fetch_plan`:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If the synchronous dependency is unavoidable, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the loop is not held.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters across an await without _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes back `current + cost` on line 19 — all without acquiring `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) holds for exactly this state.

Two concrete defects follow:

1. Limit bypass: any number of coroutines can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 with the same stale `current`, suspend at line 18, and then each commit its own cost. The effective counter can exceed `LIMIT` by an unbounded multiple of `cost`.
2. Lost update: line 19 assigns an absolute value computed from a stale read rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call (or another `try_consume`) that completed during the suspension is silently overwritten and its cost disappears from the counter — so `_lock` no longer makes `consume` atomic either.

Fix by holding the lock for the whole read-check-write, e.g. `async with _lock:` wrapping lines 15-20, and re-reading the counter after any suspension inside it (or removing the `await` from the critical section entirely and incrementing with `_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act on _counters without _lock

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in billing/gateway.py as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." The gateway docstring names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge (outside the retried function, so all attempts share it) and thread it through `charge()` so the gateway collapses retries into a single charge. Until that key is plumbed through, this function should not be retried automatically. Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7, which wraps `get_charge` \u2014 documented as "Safe to repeat" \u2014 and is correctly retryable.
